For the five‑step dehydrogenation sequence the elementary rates are  

\[
\begin{aligned}
r_1 &=k_1\,\theta_{\rm EtOH},\\
r_2 &=k_2\,\theta_{\rm EtO},\\
r_3 &=k_3\,\theta_{\rm EtO^*},\\
r_4 &=k_4\,\theta_{\rm EtCO},\\
r_5 &=k_5\,\theta_{\rm CH_3CO},
\end{aligned}
\]

where \(\theta_i\) denotes the fractional coverage of the corresponding surface intermediate.  
Under the steady–state approximation each intermediate is produced and consumed at the same rate, i.e.

\[
r_1=r_2=r_3=r_4=r_5\equiv {\rm TOF}.
\]

Hence  

\[
\theta_{\rm EtOH}= \frac{{\rm TOF}}{k_1},\qquad
\theta_{\rm EtO}= \frac{{\rm TOF}}{k_2},\qquad
\theta_{\rm EtO^*}= \frac{{\rm TOF}}{k_3},
\]
\[
\theta_{\rm EtCO}= \frac{{\rm TOF}}{k_4},\qquad
\theta_{\rm CH_3CO}= \frac{{\rm TOF}}{k_5}.
\]

The total fraction of Rh sites that are occupied at any instant is the sum of the coverages of all surface species.  Because each Rh site can be in only one of these states, the sum of the fractional occupancies must be equal to the fraction of time a site spends occupied during one catalytic cycle:

\[
\theta_{\rm EtOH}+\theta_{\rm EtO}+\theta_{\rm EtO^*}+\theta_{\rm EtCO}
+\theta_{\rm CH_3CO}= {\rm TOF}\!\left(\frac1{k_1}+\frac1{k_2}+\frac1{k_3}
+\frac1{k_4}+\frac1{k_5}\right).
\]

A catalytic turnover corresponds to one complete passage of a Rh site through the five states; the total time required for one cycle is therefore

\[
\tau_{\rm cycle}= \frac1{k_1}+\frac1{k_2}+\frac1{k_3}+\frac1{k_4}+\frac1{k_5}.
\]

The turnover frequency (cycles per Rh site per unit time) is the inverse of this total cycle time:

\[
\boxed{{\rm TOF}= \frac{1}{\displaystyle\frac1{k_1}+\frac1{k_2}+\frac1{k_3}
+\frac1{k_4}+\frac1{k_5}} }.
\]

Equivalently, after clearing the denominator,

\[
\boxed{{\rm TOF}= \frac{k_1k_2k_3k_4k_5}
{k_2k_3k_4k_5+k_1k_3k_4k_5+k_1k_2k_4k_5+k_1k_2k_3k_5+k_1k_2k_3k_4}}.
\]

If the coverage of the initially adsorbed ethanol is expressed through a Langmuir adsorption equilibrium, \(\theta_{\rm EtOH}=K_{\rm EtOH}\,p_{\rm EtOH}\), the TOF per Rh site becomes  

\[
{\rm TOF}= \frac{K_{\rm EtOH}\,p_{\rm EtOH}}
{\displaystyle\frac1{k_1}+\frac1{k_2}+\frac1{k_3}+\frac1{k_4}+\frac1{k_5}} .
\]

The required analytical expression for the overall turnover frequency is therefore the harmonic sum of the five elementary first‑order rate constants, as shown above.

**Derivation**

For the reversible reaction  

\[
\mathrm{A+CO_2+H_2O\;\rightleftharpoons\;C^-+{\rm H^+}+RNH_3^+}
\]

the thermodynamic equilibrium constant is  

\[
K_{\rm eq}
=\frac{[C^-][RNH_3^+][\mathrm{H^+}]}{[A][\mathrm{CO_2(aq)}]}
\equiv\frac{[C][\mathrm{H^+}]}{[A][\mathrm{CO_2(aq)}]},
\]

where we have introduced the neutral “carbamate surfactant’’ concentration  

\[
[C]\equiv[C^-][RNH_3^+].
\]

Because the solution is buffered at pH ≈ 12, \([\mathrm{H^+}]\) is essentially constant.  Define  

\[
K'\equiv\frac{K_{\rm eq}}{[\mathrm{H^+}]}
      =\frac{[C]}{[A][\mathrm{CO_2(aq)}]} .
\tag{1}
\]

Let the total surfactant concentration be  

\[
C_{\rm tot}= [A]+[C].
\tag{2}
\]

From (1) we have  

\[
[C]=K'\,[\mathrm{CO_2(aq)}]\,[A]
    =K'\,[\mathrm{CO_2(aq)}]\,(C_{\rm tot}-[C]).
\]

Solving for \([C]\),

\[
[C]\bigl(1+K'[\mathrm{CO_2(aq)}]\bigr)
      =K'[\mathrm{CO_2(aq)}]\,C_{\rm tot}
\;\;\Longrightarrow\;\;
[C]=\frac{K'[\mathrm{CO_2(aq)}]}{1+K'[\mathrm{CO_2(aq)}]}\;C_{\rm tot}.
\]

Hence the equilibrium fraction of surfactant present as the carbamate,  

\[
f_C^{\rm eq}\equiv\frac{[C]}{C_{\rm tot}}
                =\frac{K'[\mathrm{CO_2(aq)}]}{1+K'[\mathrm{CO_2(aq)}]} .
\tag{3}
\]

The dissolved CO₂ obeys Henry’s law  

\[
[\mathrm{CO_2(aq)}]=k_H\,p_{\mathrm{CO_2}} .
\tag{4}
\]

At equilibrium the forward and reverse kinetic rates are equal:

\[
k_f[\mathrm{CO_2(aq)}][A]=k_r[C]
\;\;\Longrightarrow\;\;
\frac{[C]}{[A]}=\frac{k_f}{k_r}\,[\mathrm{CO_2(aq)}].
\]

Comparing with (1) gives  

\[
K'=\frac{k_f}{k_r}.
\tag{5}
\]

Substituting (4) and (5) into (3) yields the desired expression:

\[
\boxed{%
f_C^{\rm eq}
   =\frac{(k_f/k_r)\;k_H\;p_{\mathrm{CO_2}}}
          {1+(k_f/k_r)\;k_H\;p_{\mathrm{CO_2}}}
   =\frac{K_{\rm eq}\,k_H\,p_{\mathrm{CO_2}}/[\mathrm{H^+}]}
          {1+K_{\rm eq}\,k_H\,p_{\mathrm{CO_2}}/[\mathrm{H^+}]}
}.
\]

Thus the equilibrium fraction of the total surfactant that is present as the carbamate \(C\) depends only on the CO₂ partial pressure, Henry’s constant, and the kinetic (or thermodynamic) constant \(k_f/k_r\) (or equivalently \(K_{\rm eq}/[\mathrm{H^+}]\)).

I_i=C\,\underbrace{|E_{\rm loc}(\omega_{\rm in},\theta)|^{2}\,
|E_{\rm loc}(\omega_{\rm out},\theta)|^{2}}_{\displaystyle\text{EM factor}}\;
\sigma_i^{(0)}\,
\underbrace{\eta_i(d)}_{\displaystyle\text{chemical}} .
\]

Hence the overall enhancement factor that multiplies the intrinsic Raman
cross‑section is  

\[
G_i(d,\theta)=|E_{\rm loc}(\omega_{\rm in},\theta)|^{2}\,
|E_{\rm loc}(\omega_{\rm out},\theta)|^{2}\,
\eta_i(d).
\]

---

### Electromagnetic part  

The local field at a distance \(z=d\) from the metal surface is the product
of the incident field amplitude, the SPP‑coupling efficiency (Lorentzian),
and the evanescent decay:

\[
|E_{\rm loc}(\omega_{\rm in},\theta)|
=|E_0|\,
\frac{\Gamma}{\sqrt{\Delta(\theta)^2+\Gamma^{2}}}\,
e^{-d/\lambda_{\rm sp}} .
\]

For the scattered frequency we take the same exponential decay (the Raman
shift is small, so the Lorentzian factor can be approximated by the same
value). Thus  

\[
|E_{\rm loc}(\omega_{\rm out},\theta)|
\simeq |E_0|\,
e^{-d/\lambda_{\rm sp}} .
\]

Consequently  

\[
|E_{\rm loc}(\omega_{\rm in},\theta)|^{2}
|E_{\rm loc}(\omega_{\rm out},\theta)|^{2}
=|E_0|^{4}\,
\frac{\Gamma^{2}}{\Delta(\theta)^{2}+\Gamma^{2}}\,
\frac{\Gamma^{2}}{\Delta(\theta)^{2}+\Gamma^{2}}\,
e^{-4d/\lambda_{\rm sp}}
=|E_0|^{4}\,
\frac{\Gamma^{4}}{\big[\Delta(\theta)^{2}+\Gamma^{2}\big]^{2}}\,
e^{-4d/\lambda_{\rm sp}} .
\]

---

### Chemical part  

\[
\eta_i(d)=\eta_i^{(0)}\,e^{-\alpha_i d}.
\]

---

### Overall SERS enhancement  

Multiplying the EM and chemical contributions gives  

\[
\boxed{
G_i(d,\theta)=
\eta_i^{(0)}\,|E_0|^{4}\,
\frac{\Gamma^{4}}{\big[\Delta(\theta)^{2}+\Gamma^{2}\big]^{2}}\,
\exp\!\Big[-\Big(\frac{4}{\lambda_{\rm sp}}+\alpha_i\Big)d\Big]
}
\]

or, written as a product of the two separate contributions,

\[
\boxed{
G_i(d,\theta)=
\underbrace{|E_0|^{4}\,
\frac{\Gamma^{4}}{\big[\Delta(\theta)^{2}+\Gamma^{2}\big]^{2}}\,
e^{-4d/\lambda_{\rm sp}}}_{\text{electromagnetic}}
\;
\underbrace{\eta_i^{(0)}\,e^{-\alpha_i d}}_{\text{chemical}} .
}
\]

This factor multiplies the intrinsic Raman cross‑section \(\sigma_i^{(0)}\) in the expression \(I_i=C\,G_i(d,\theta)\,\sigma_i^{(0)}\).

During sliding, tribochemical reactions can occur at the interface, and the ambient atmosphere may contain water vapor (partial pressure *p*ₕ₂ₒ).

1. **Fluorine transfer:**  
   Al–O + CF₂ → Al–F + •CF (radical)  ΔE₁ (reaction energy)  

2. **C–F bond scission and double‑bond formation:**  
   •CF + Al–F → Al–CF + F  ΔE₂  

3. **Hydration of the terminal double bond:**  
   Al–CF + H₂O → Al–COOH + HF  ΔE₃

|----------|-----------|----------|
| 1        | –1.20     | 0.30     |
| 2        | –0.45     | 0.20     |
| 3        | –0.80     | 0.15     |

A tetra‑functional epoxy resin **E** (four epoxide groups per molecule) is cured with a mixture of a primary diamine **A** (tetra‑gly‑cidyl‑dimethyl‑diaminodiphenylmethane, TGDDM) and a secondary diamine **B** (diaminodiphenylsulfone, DDS).  The cure proceeds through three elementary pathways  

1. **Primary amine–epoxide addition**  \(E + A \xrightarrow{k_{1}} P_{1}\)  (ΔH₁ < 0)  
2. **Secondary amine–epoxide addition** \(E + B \xrightarrow{k_{2}} P_{2}\)  (ΔH₂ < 0)  
3. **Etherification (epoxy–epoxy) reaction** \(E + E \xrightarrow{k_{3}} P_{3}\)  (ΔH₃ < 0)  

A carbon filler is incorporated at a mass fraction **w_f**.  The filler surface bears acidic groups that (i) adsorb the primary diamine **A** according to a Langmuir isotherm with equilibrium constant \(K_{\mathrm{ads}}\) (units L mol⁻¹), and (ii) act as a heterogeneous catalyst that multiplies the primary‑amine rate constant by a factor **α > 1** (i.e., \(k_{1}^{\prime}=αk_{1}\)).  

In addition, a latent Lewis‑acid catalyst **C** (e.g., BF₃·ethylamine) is present.  The catalyst is activated by the acidic filler surface but is deactivated by water adsorbed on the same surface.  The deactivation follows first‑order kinetics with respect to the active catalyst concentration, with rate constant \(k_{d}=k_{d}^{0}\,a_{w}\), where \(a_{w}\) is the water activity (0 ≤ a_w ≤ 1).  When active, the catalyst enhances the epoxy‑epoxy etherification rate by a factor **β > 1** (i.e., \(k_{3}^{\prime}=βk_{3}\)).  

The system is initially at temperature **T₀** and the cure is isothermal (temperature held constant).  The total initial molar concentrations (per unit volume) are  

\[ [E]_{0}=c_{E},\qquad [A]_{0}=c_{A},\qquad [B]_{0}=c_{B},\qquad [C]_{0}=c_{C}.\]  

Assume the following:  

* Adsorption of **A** on the filler surface is rapid relative to the chemical reactions, so that the surface concentration \([A]_{s}\) satisfies the Langmuir relation  

\[ [A]_{s}= \frac{K_{\mathrm{ads}}\,w_{f}\,[A]}{1+K_{\mathrm{ads}}\,w_{f}\,[A]} .\]  

* Only the *free* (non‑adsorbed) primary amine participates in the bulk primary‑amine reaction, i.e. the effective concentration of reactive **A** is \([A]_{\text{eff}}=[A]-[A]_{s}\).  

* The catalyst **C** is present only in the bulk; its activation by the filler surface is instantaneous, so that the active catalyst concentration is simply \([C]_{\text{act}}=[C]\) as long as it has not been deactivated by water.  

* The cure exotherm is the sum of the heats released by each elementary reaction, proportional to their instantaneous rates.

\[\frac{1}{T_{g}}=\frac{1-\xi}{T_{g,0}}+\frac{\xi}{T_{g,\infty}}\]  

to obtain an expression for the glass‑transition temperature \(T_{g}(\xi)\) as a function of the overall conversion \(\xi\).  Define \(\xi\) in terms of the stoichiometric consumption of epoxide groups.

**Derivation**

1. **Adsorption equilibria (quasi‑equilibrium)**  

\[
\theta_{\rm CO}=K_{\rm CO}\,p_{\rm CO}\,\theta_* ,\qquad 
\theta_{\rm NO}=K_{\rm NO}\,p_{\rm NO}\,\theta_* .
\]

2. **Rate‑determining step**  

The slow step is  

\[
{\rm NO}^*\;\xrightarrow{k_3}\;{\rm N}^*+{\rm O}^* .
\]

Hence the rate of CO₂ formation (which follows the RDS) is  

\[
r_{\rm CO_2}=k_3\,\theta_{\rm NO}.
\tag{1}
\]

3. **Site balance**  

\[
\theta_*+\theta_{\rm CO}+\theta_{\rm NO}+\theta_{\rm N}+\theta_{\rm O}=1 .
\tag{2}
\]

4. **Steady state for the reactive intermediate O\***  

O* is consumed in the fast step  

\[
{\rm CO}^*+{\rm O}^*\;\xrightarrow{k_4}\;{\rm CO_2}^*+* .
\]

Thus  

\[
\frac{d\theta_{\rm O}}{dt}=k_3\theta_{\rm NO}-k_4\theta_{\rm CO}\theta_{\rm O}=0
\;\Longrightarrow\;
\theta_{\rm O}= \frac{k_3}{k_4}\,\frac{\theta_{\rm NO}}{\theta_{\rm CO}}
          =\frac{k_3}{k_4}\,\frac{K_{\rm NO}\,p_{\rm NO}}{K_{\rm CO}\,p_{\rm CO}} .
\tag{3}
\]

The coverage of N* does not appear in any subsequent step; it is assumed to be removed (or to remain very small) so that \(\theta_{\rm N}\approx0\).

5. **Solve for the fraction of vacant sites \(\theta_*\)**  

Insert (3) and the adsorption relations into the site balance (2):

\[
\theta_* \Bigl[1+K_{\rm CO}p_{\rm CO}+K_{\rm NO}p_{\rm NO}\Bigr]
      =1-\theta_{\rm O}
      =1-\frac{k_3}{k_4}\,\frac{K_{\rm NO}p_{\rm NO}}{K_{\rm CO}p_{\rm CO}} .
\]

Hence  

\[
\theta_*=
\frac{1-\displaystyle\frac{k_3}{k_4}\,
      \frac{K_{\rm NO}p_{\rm NO}}{K_{\rm CO}p_{\rm CO}}}
     {1+K_{\rm CO}p_{\rm CO}+K_{\rm NO}p_{\rm NO}} .
\tag{4}
\]

6. **Rate expression**  

Using (1) together with \(\theta_{\rm NO}=K_{\rm NO}p_{\rm NO}\theta_*\) and (4),

\[
r_{\rm CO_2}=k_3\,K_{\rm NO}p_{\rm NO}\,
\frac{1-\displaystyle\frac{k_3}{k_4}\,
      \frac{K_{\rm NO}p_{\rm NO}}{K_{\rm CO}p_{\rm CO}}}
     {1+K_{\rm CO}p_{\rm CO}+K_{\rm NO}p_{\rm NO}} .
\tag{5}
\]

7. **Arrhenius form of the RDS rate constant**  

\[
k_3 = k_3^{0}\,\exp\!\bigl(-E_a/RT\bigr) .
\]

Substituting this into (5) gives the explicit Langmuir–Hinshelwood rate law for a given surface termination \(i\) (i = A or B):

\[
r_{\rm CO_2}^{(i)}=
\frac{k_3^{0}\exp\!\bigl(-E_a^{(i)}/RT\bigr)\,
      K_{\rm NO}^{(i)}p_{\rm NO}}
     {1+K_{\rm CO}^{(i)}p_{\rm CO}+K_{\rm NO}^{(i)}p_{\rm NO}}
\Biggl[1-
\frac{k_3^{0}\exp\!\bigl(-E_a^{(i)}/RT\bigr)}{k_4}\,
\frac{K_{\rm NO}^{(i)}p_{\rm NO}}{K_{\rm CO}^{(i)}p_{\rm CO}}
\Biggr].
\]

Because step 4 is much faster than the RDS (\(k_4\gg k_3\)), the term in brackets is ≈ 1, and the familiar LH form is recovered:

\[
\boxed{
r_{\rm CO_2}^{(i)}\;=\;
\frac{k_3^{0}\,\exp\!\bigl(-E_a^{(i)}/RT\bigr)\;
      K_{\rm NO}^{(i)}\,p_{\rm NO}}
     {1\;+\;K_{\rm CO}^{(i)}\,p_{\rm CO}
        \;+\;K_{\rm NO}^{(i)}\,p_{\rm NO}}
}
\]

The rate explicitly contains the surface coverages through the term
\(\theta_{\rm NO}=K_{\rm NO}^{(i)}p_{\rm NO}\theta_*\) (and, via the site balance,
the coverages of CO*, O* and N*). This expression applies separately to terminations A and B by using the corresponding \(K_{\rm CO}^{(i)}\), \(K_{\rm NO}^{(i)}\) and activation energy \(E_a^{(i)}\).

The linear‐stability result for a permeability jump is  

\[
\Gamma \;\propto\; \frac{k_{2}}{k_{1}}\Big(M_{\rm eff}-1\Big) .
\]

Viscous fingering is just suppressed when \(\Gamma=0\); therefore  

\[
M_{\rm eff}=1 .
\]

The “effective’’ mobility ratio across the two adjacent blocks is the ratio of the
total mobility of the displacing gas in the high‑permeability block to the total
mobility of the displaced oil in the low‑permeability block:

\[
M_{\rm eff}= \frac{k_{2}\,\lambda_{g}}{k_{1}\,\lambda_{o}}
           =\frac{k_{2}}{k_{1}}\;
             \frac{k_{rg}/\mu_{g}}{k_{ro}/\mu_{o}}
           =\frac{k_{2}}{k_{1}}\;
             \frac{k_{rg}\,\mu_{o}}{k_{ro}\,\mu_{g}} .
\]

Setting \(M_{\rm eff}=1\) gives the condition for the permeability ratio that
just stabilises the front:

\[
\frac{k_{2}}{k_{1}}=
\frac{k_{ro}\,\mu_{g}}{k_{rg}\,\mu_{o}} .
\]

Writing the contrast as \(\Delta k/k\equiv (k_{2}-k_{1})/k_{1}=k_{2}/k_{1}-1\),

\[
\boxed{\;
\frac{\Delta k}{k}\Big|_{\rm crit}
    =\frac{k_{ro}\,\mu_{g}}{k_{rg}\,\mu_{o}}-1
\;}
\tag{1}
\]

---

At the displacement front the effective water saturation is zero
(\(S_{we}=0\)), so  

\[
k_{ro}=k_{ro0}=0.8,\qquad 
k_{rg}=k_{rg0}=0.2 .
\]

The oil viscosity is \(\mu_{o}=5\;{\rm cP}\) and the gas viscosity varies with the
CO\(_2\) mole fraction:

\[
\mu_{g}= \mu_{g0}\,(1-X_{\rm CO_2})^{\beta},
\qquad 
\mu_{g0}=0.07\;{\rm cP},\;\beta=0.3 .
\]

Insert these into (1):

\[
\frac{\Delta k}{k}\Big|_{\rm crit}
   =\frac{0.8\,\mu_{g}}{0.2\times5}-1
   =0.8\,\mu_{g}-1
   =0.8\,\mu_{g0}\,(1-X_{\rm CO_2})^{0.3}-1 .
\]

\[

\]

\qquad

\]

\[

= -\frac{\alpha\lambda e\psi_{0}}{b}
+2\beta k_{B}T\frac{\delta}{R_{g}^{2}}=0,

\[

\[

\delta_{\rm eq}= \frac{\alpha\lambda e\psi_{0}\,b\,N^{2\nu}}{2\beta k_{B}T}
= \frac{\alpha\lambda e\psi_{0}\,b\,N^{1.2}}{2\beta k_{B}T}\; }.

\[
\theta=\frac{K_{L}C_{e}}{1+K_{L}C_{e}}
\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad
\frac{C_{e}}{\theta}= \frac{1}{K_{L}}+C_{e}
\]

A plot of \(C_{e}/\theta\) versus \(C_{e}\) gives a straight line whose intercept is \(1/K_{L}\).

| \(C_{e}\) (mol L\(^{-1}\)) | \(\theta\) | \(C_{e}/\theta\) (mol L\(^{-1}\)) |
|---------------------------|------------|-----------------------------------|
| \(1.0\times10^{-6}\)      | 0.12       | \(8.33\times10^{-6}\) |
| \(5.0\times10^{-6}\)      | 0.45       | \(1.11\times10^{-5}\) |
| \(2.0\times10^{-5}\)      | 0.78       | \(2.56\times10^{-5}\) |
| \(5.0\times10^{-5}\)      | 0.95       | \(5.26\times10^{-5}\) |

Linear regression of \(y=C_{e}/\theta\) vs. \(x=C_{e}\) yields  

\[
y = (7.10\times10^{-6}) + (0.912)\,x .
\]

Thus  

\[
\frac{1}{K_{L}} = 7.10\times10^{-6}\;\text{L mol}^{-1}
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
K_{L}= \frac{1}{7.10\times10^{-6}}
      \approx 1.4\times10^{5}\;\text{L mol}^{-1}.
\]

The standard free‑energy change for adsorption is

\[
\Delta G^{\circ}_{\text{ads}} = -RT\ln K_{L},
\]

with \(R = 8.314\;\text{J mol}^{-1}\text{K}^{-1}\) and \(T = 298\;\text{K}\):

\[
\ln K_{L}= \ln(1.4\times10^{5})\approx 11.86,

\[

                               \approx -2.94\times10^{4}\;\text{J mol}^{-1}
                               = -29\;\text{kJ mol}^{-1}.
\]

\[

**Derivation**

For a first‑order surface reaction (or desorption)

\[
r(T)= -\frac{d\theta}{dt}=k(T)\,\theta
      =\nu\,\theta\,\exp\!\Big(-\frac{E}{RT}\Big) .
\]

During a linear temperature ramp  

\[
T(t)=T_{0}+\beta t ,\qquad \beta=\frac{dT}{dt}\;,
\]

so that  

\[
\frac{d\theta}{dT}= \frac{d\theta}{dt}\frac{dt}{dT}
                 =-\frac{\nu}{\beta}\,\theta\,
                   \exp\!\Big(-\frac{E}{RT}\Big) .
\]

The peak temperature \(T_{p}\) is defined by the maximum of the rate,
\(dr/dT=0\).  Using  

\[
r(T)=\nu\,\theta(T)\exp\!\Big(-\frac{E}{RT}\Big)
\]

gives  

\[
\frac{dr}{dT}= \nu\exp\!\Big(-\frac{E}{RT}\Big)
               \Big[\,\frac{d\theta}{dT}
                     -\theta\frac{E}{RT^{2}}\,\Big]=0 .
\]

Substituting the expression for \(d\theta/dT\) yields the condition at
\(T=T_{p}\)

\[
\frac{E}{R\,T_{p}^{2}}=\frac{\nu}{\beta}
      \exp\!\Big(-\frac{E}{R\,T_{p}}\Big) .
\tag{1}
\]

Re‑arranging (1),

\[
\frac{E}{R\,T_{p}}=
   \ln\!\Big(\frac{\nu R\,T_{p}^{2}}{\beta E}\Big)
   =\ln\!\Big(\frac{\nu T_{p}}{\beta}\Big)
    -\ln\!\Big(\frac{E}{R\,T_{p}}\Big) .
\tag{2}
\]

Define \(x\equiv E/(R\,T_{p})\); then (2) becomes  

\[
x+\ln x=\ln\!\Big(\frac{\nu T_{p}}{\beta}\Big) .
\tag{3}
\]

For typical first‑order desorption \(x\) lies in the range 30–40, so
\(\ln x\approx3.64\).  Inserting this constant into (3) gives the
Redhead approximation

\[
x\;\approx\;\ln\!\Big(\frac{\nu T_{p}}{\beta}\Big)-3.64 .
\]

Finally, restoring \(x=E/(R\,T_{p})\),

\[
\boxed{\;
\frac{E}{R\,T_{p}}\;\approx\;
\ln\!\Big(\frac{\nu\,T_{p}}{\beta}\Big)-3.64
\;}
\qquad\text{or equivalently}\qquad
\boxed{\;
T_{p}\;\approx\;
\frac{E}{R\big[\ln(\nu T_{p}/\beta)-3.64\big]}
\;}
\]

Thus the peak temperature depends logarithmically on the pre‑exponential
factor \(\nu\) and the heating rate \(\beta\), and linearly on the
activation energy \(E\).  (Equation (1) or the implicit form
\(T_{p}=E/[R\ln(\nu R T_{p}^{2}/\beta E)]\) is exact; the boxed
expressions are the widely used Redhead approximations.)

\[

\theta_{A}+\theta_{P}+\theta_{\text{Cl}}=1 .

\theta_{\text{Cl}}\bigl(1+K_{A}[A]+K_{P}[P]\bigr)=1

A clay mineral (Ca‑montmorillonite) is investigated as a sorbent for divalent cadmium ions (Cd²⁺) in aqueous solution. Batch sorption experiments are performed at three temperatures (298 K, 313 K, and 328 K) over a range of pH values (4–11) and ionic strengths (0.01 M and 0.1 M NaCl). The equilibrium data are fitted to the Langmuir isotherm

q_e = q_max K_L C_e / (1 + K_L C_e)

where q_e (mg g⁻¹) is the amount of Cd²⁺ adsorbed, C_e (mg L⁻¹) the equilibrium concentration, q_max the maximum adsorption capacity, and K_L the Langmuir affinity constant.

The following Langmuir parameters are obtained at pH = 6 (low pH) and pH = 9 (high pH) for the 0.01 M ionic strength condition:

| Temperature (K) | pH | q_max (mg g⁻¹) | K_L (L mg⁻¹) |
|-----------------|----|----------------|--------------|
| 298             | 6  | 12.5           | 0.45         |
| 313             | 6  | 13.2           | 0.62         |
| 328             | 6  | 14.0           | 0.85         |
| 298             | 9  | 18.3           | 1.10         |
| 313             | 9  | 19.5           | 1.45         |
| 328             | 9  | 20.8           | 1.92         |

Assume that the Langmuir affinity constant K_L is related to the standard Gibbs free energy change for sorption by

ΔG° = -RT ln K_L,

where R = 8.314 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹.

**(a)** Using the data at pH = 6, calculate the standard enthalpy (ΔH°) and entropy (ΔS°) changes for Cd²⁺ sorption on Ca‑montmorillonite. Show all steps, including the linearization of the van’t Hoff equation.

\[
\ln K_L \;=\;-\frac{\Delta H^{\circ}}{R}\,\frac{1}{T}+\frac{\Delta S^{\circ}}{R}
\]

Thus a plot of \(\ln K_L\) versus \(1/T\) gives a straight line whose  

* slope \(m=-\Delta H^{\circ}/R\)  
* intercept \(b=\Delta S^{\circ}/R\).

---

| \(T\) (K) | \(K_L\) (L mg⁻¹) | \(\displaystyle \frac{1}{T}\) (K⁻¹) | \(\displaystyle \ln K_L\) |
|-----------|----------------|----------------------|-------------------|
| 298 | 0.45 | 0.0033557047 | –0.7985077 |
| 313 | 0.62 | 0.0031948882 | –0.4780358 |
| 328 | 0.85 | 0.0030487805 | –0.1625189 |

---

### 2.  Linear regression ( \(\ln K_L = m(1/T)+b\) )

\[
\begin{aligned}
\Sigma x &=0.0095993734\\
\Sigma y &=-1.4390624\\
\Sigma x^2 &=3.076306\times10^{-5}\\
\Sigma xy &=-0.004702307\\
N &=3
\end{aligned}
\]

\[
m=\frac{N\Sigma xy-\Sigma x\,\Sigma y}{N\Sigma x^{2}-(\Sigma x)^{2}}

            {3(3.076306\times10^{-5})-(0.0095993734)^{2}}
      =-2.08\times10^{3}\;{\rm K}
\]

\[
b=\frac{\Sigma y-m\Sigma x}{N}
   =\frac{-1.4390624-(-2.08\times10^{3})(0.0095993734)}{3}
   =6.19
\]

---

### 3.  Obtain \(\Delta H^{\circ}\) and \(\Delta S^{\circ}\)

\[
\begin{aligned}
\Delta H^{\circ}&=-mR

               &\approx+1.73\times10^{4}\;{\rm J\,mol^{-1}}
               =+17.3\;{\rm kJ\,mol^{-1}}\\[4pt]
\Delta S^{\circ}&=bR
               =6.19\,(8.314\;{\rm J\,mol^{-1}\,K^{-1}})\\
               &\approx+5.1\times10^{1}\;{\rm J\,mol^{-1}\,K^{-1}}
\end{aligned}
\]

---

\[
\boxed{\displaystyle \Delta H^{\circ}\;\approx\;+\;17\;\text{kJ mol}^{-1},
\qquad
\Delta S^{\circ}\;\approx\;+\;5.1\times10^{1}\;\text{J mol}^{-1}\text{K}^{-1}}

| I₂     | 0.5                               | 1.9                        |
| I₂     | 2.0                               | 2.5                        |
| I₂     | 5.0                               | 2.9                        |

Assume that the adsorption of each halogen follows a Langmuir isotherm of the form  

q = \frac{q_{\max} K C}{1 + K C}

\[

\text{H}_2\text{O}(g)+* &\rightleftharpoons \text{H}_2\text{O}* \qquad K_{\rm H_2O}=K_{\rm H_2O}P_{\rm H_2O}\,\theta_* .
\end{aligned}
\]

With negligible coverage by carbonaceous intermediates the site‑balance is  

\[
\theta_*+\theta_{\rm CH_4}+\theta_{\rm H_2O}=1 .
\]

\[
\theta_*=\frac{1}{1+K_{\rm CH_4}P_{\rm CH_4}+K_{\rm H_2O}P_{\rm H_2O}},
\qquad

\frac{K_{\rm CH_4}P_{\rm CH_4}}
{1+K_{\rm CH_4}P_{\rm CH_4}+K_{\rm H_2O}P_{\rm H_2O}} .
\]

The rate‑determining step is the dehydrogenation of adsorbed methane, so the rate per *active site* is  

\[
r_{\text{site}}=k\,\theta_{\rm CH_4}\;(\text{mol\,site}^{-1}\,\text{s}^{-1}) .
\]

\[
N_{\rm Ni}= \Gamma_{\rm Ni}\,a_{\rm ext}\qquad

a_{\rm ext}= \text{external surface area (m}^2\text{ g}^{-1})\bigr),
\]

\[

r = k\,N_{\rm Ni}\,\frac{K_{\rm CH_4}P_{\rm CH_4}}
{1+K_{\rm CH_4}P_{\rm CH_4}+K_{\rm H_2O}P_{\rm H_2O}}

\frac{K_{\rm CH_4}P_{\rm CH_4}}
{1+K_{\rm CH_4}P_{\rm CH_4}+K_{\rm H_2O}P_{\rm H_2O}}%
}
\]

which explicitly incorporates the finite number of surface Ni sites through the measured surface concentration \(\Gamma_{\rm Ni}\).  (If the catalyst’s external surface area per gram, \(a_{\rm ext}\), is known, the numerical value of \(r\) follows directly.)

The Raman intensity from a given phase is proportional to its scattering cross‑section times the number of scattering sites that lie within the probed surface layer.

\[
V_{\text{shell}}= \frac{4\pi}{3}\Big[ R_{p}^{3}-(R_{p}-\delta)^{3}\Big]

\]

is the volume of the probed surface shell.

\[
V_{a}=f_{a}\,V_{\text{shell}},\qquad

\]

\[
I_{a}\propto \sigma_{a}\,V_{a}= \sigma_{a}\,f_{a}\,V_{\text{shell}},
\qquad
I_{r}\propto \sigma_{r}\,V_{r}= \sigma_{r}\,f_{r}\,V_{\text{shell}} .
\]

\[
\boxed{R\;=\;\frac{I_{a}}{I_{r}}
      =\frac{\sigma_{a}}{\sigma_{r}}\,

\]

### Part (e) – Dual‑site kinetic model for alkyne semihydrogenation
A nickel phosphide catalyst mediates the semihydrogenation of a terminal alkyne (A–C≡C–H) to the corresponding alkene (A–C=CH₂). A **dual‑site mechanism** is proposed:

* **Site A** adsorbs the alkyne molecularly: \( 	ext{A} + 	ext{S}_A ightleftharpoons 	ext{A–S}_A \) with adsorption equilibrium constant \(K_A\).
* **Site B** dissociatively adsorbs hydrogen: \( 	ext{H}_2 + 2	ext{S}_B ightleftharpoons 2	ext{H–S}_B \) with equilibrium constant \(K_{H_2}\).

The **rate‑determining step** is the surface reaction between the adsorbed alkyne and a surface hydrogen atom:

\[ 	ext{A–S}_A + 	ext{H–S}_B \xrightarrow{k_1} 	ext{alkene–S}_A + 	ext{S}_B . \]

Assuming **Langmuir adsorption** on each site type and that the **total fraction of each site type** is unity (i.e., \(	heta_{A} + 	heta_{V,A}=1\) and \(	heta_{H} + 	heta_{V,B}=1\)), derive an expression for the **overall rate of alkene formation** \(r\) in terms of the partial pressures \(P_A\) (alkyne) and \(P_{H_2}\) (hydrogen), the constants \(K_A\), \(K_{H_2}\), and the intrinsic rate constant \(k_1\).
reasoning:
We need to derive an expression for the overall rate of alkene formation r in a dual-site kinetic model for alkyne semihydrogenation.

Given:

- Site A adsorbs alkyne molecularly: A + S_A ⇌ A–S_A with adsorption equilibrium constant K_A.

- Site B dissociatively adsorbs hydrogen: H2 + 2 S_B ⇌ 2 H–S_B with equilibrium constant K_{H2}.

- Rate-determining step: A–S_A + H–S_B → alkene–S_A + S_B, with intrinsic rate constant k1.

Assume Langmuir adsorption on each site type and total fraction of each site type is unity: θ_A + θ_{V,A} = 1 and θ_H + θ_{V,B} = 1.

We need to derive expression for overall rate of alkene formation r in terms of partial pressures P_A (alkyne) and P_{H2} (hydrogen), constants K_A, K_{H2}, and k1.

We need to consider the surface coverages.

Define:

- θ_{A} = fraction of type A sites occupied by alkyne (i.e., A–S_A). θ_{V,A} = fraction of type A sites vacant.

- θ_{H} = fraction of type B sites occupied by hydrogen (i.e., H–S_B). θ_{V,B} = fraction of type B sites vacant.

From Langmuir adsorption:

- For site A: K_A = θ_{A} / (P_A * θ_{V,A}) => θ_{A} = K_A P_A θ_{V,A}.

Since θ_{A} + θ_{V,A} = 1 => θ_{V,A} = 1 - θ_{A}.

Thus θ_{A} = K_A P_A (1 - θ_{A}) => θ_{A} = K_A P_A - K_A P_A θ_{A} => θ_{A} (1 + K_A P_A) = K_A P_A => θ_{A} = K_A P_A / (1 + K_A P_A). Similarly, θ_{V,A} = 1/(1 + K_A P_A).

- For site B: Dissociative adsorption of H2: H2 + 2 S_B ⇌ 2 H–S_B. The equilibrium constant K_{H2} relates to the coverage of H–S_B. For dissociative adsorption, we need to write equilibrium expression: K_{H2} = (θ_H)^2 / (P_{H2} * (θ_{V,B})^2). Since each H2 yields 2 H atoms occupying 2 sites.

**Derivation of the kinetic‐isotope selectivity**

The initial uptake rate per gram of adsorbent for isotope \(i\) is  

\[
r_i(R)=\frac{S}{A_{\rm site}}\;D_i(R)\;\frac{P}{RT},
\qquad 
D_i(R)=D_0\exp\!\Big[-\frac{E_{a,i}(R)}{RT}\Big].
\]

Because the geometric factor \(S/A_{\rm site}\) and the term \(P/(RT)\) are identical for H\(_2\) and D\(_2\), they cancel in the ratio

\[
\mathcal{S}^{\rm kin}(R)=\frac{r_{\rm D}(R)}{r_{\rm H}(R)}
   =\frac{D_{\rm D}(R)}{D_{\rm H}(R)}
   =\frac{\exp[-E_{a,{\rm D}}(R)/(RT)]}
          {\exp[-E_{a,{\rm H}}(R)/(RT)]}
   =\exp\!\Big[\frac{E_{a,{\rm H}}(R)-E_{a,{\rm D}}(R)}{RT}\Big].
\]

The activation energy for diffusion is

\[
E_{a,i}(R)=E_0+\frac{\beta}{R^{2}}-\gamma m_i .
\]

Hence

\[
E_{a,{\rm H}}(R)-E_{a,{\rm D}}(R)
   =\Big(E_0+\frac{\beta}{R^{2}}-\gamma m_{\rm H}\Big)
    -\Big(E_0+\frac{\beta}{R^{2}}-\gamma m_{\rm D}\Big)
   =\gamma\,(m_{\rm D}-m_{\rm H}),
\]

i.e. the radius‑dependent terms cancel completely.  Substituting gives the **explicit kinetic isotope selectivity**

\[
\boxed{\displaystyle
\mathcal{S}^{\rm kin}(R)=\exp\!\Big[\frac{\gamma\,(m_{\rm D}-m_{\rm H})}{RT}\Big]
}.
\]

---

### Numerical evaluation ( \(T=77\;{\rm K}\) )

\[
\begin{aligned}
\gamma &=0.02\;\text{kJ mol}^{-1}\,\text{u}^{-1}
        =20\;\text{J mol}^{-1}\,\text{u}^{-1},\\[2mm]
m_{\rm D}-m_{\rm H} &=4.028-2.016=2.012\;\text{u},\\[2mm]
\gamma\,(m_{\rm D}-m_{\rm H}) &=20\times2.012=40.2\;\text{J mol}^{-1},\\[2mm]
RT &=8.314\times77=6.40\times10^{2}\;\text{J mol}^{-1},\\[2mm]
\frac{\gamma(m_{\rm D}-m_{\rm H})}{RT}&=\frac{40.2}{640}=6.29\times10^{-2},\\[2mm]
\mathcal{S}^{\rm kin}&=\exp(0.0629)=1.06\;( \text{to three significant figures} ).
\end{aligned}
\]

\[
\boxed{\mathcal{S}^{\rm kin}(R)\;\approx\;1.06}
\]

Thus, under the given model the kinetic isotope selectivity is independent of the pore radius and equals about 1.06 at 77 K.

For a binary mixture in the grand‑canonical ensemble the chemical potentials in the pore must equal those in the bulk.  Assuming the bulk fluid is ideal (so that only the ideal part contributes in the bulk) we have  

\[
\mu_i^{\rm bulk}=k_{\rm B}T\ln\!\big(y_i\rho_{\rm b}\Lambda_i^{3}\big) ,
\qquad 
\mu_i^{\rm pore}=k_{\rm B}T\ln\!\big(\rho_i^{\rm pore}\Lambda_i^{3}\big)+\mu_i^{\rm ex} .
\]

Equality \(\mu_i^{\rm bulk}=\mu_i^{\rm pore}\) gives  

\[
\rho_i^{\rm pore}=y_i\rho_{\rm b}\,
\exp\!\big[-\beta\mu_i^{\rm ex}\big] .
\]

Hence the ratio of the average numbers (or densities) in the pore is  

\[
\frac{\langle N_1\rangle}{\langle N_2\rangle}
   =\frac{y_1}{y_2}\,
   \exp\!\big[-\beta(\mu_1^{\rm ex}-\mu_2^{\rm ex})\big] .
\]

The adsorption selectivity therefore reduces to  

\[
S_{12}= \frac{\langle N_1\rangle/\langle N_2\rangle}{y_1/y_2}
      =\exp\!\big[-\beta(\mu_1^{\rm ex}-\mu_2^{\rm ex})\big] .
\tag{1}
\]

---

### SPT excess chemical potentials

For a hard‑sphere fluid confined in a cavity of volume \(V_{\rm pore}\) the SPT expression is  

\[
\beta\mu_i^{\rm ex}= -\ln(1-\eta)
   +\frac{3\eta}{1-\eta}\frac{R_i}{\langle R\rangle}
   +\frac{3\eta^{2}}{(1-\eta)^{2}}\Big(\frac{R_i}{\langle R\rangle}\Big)^{2},
\]

with \(R_i=\sigma_i/2\) and \(\langle R\rangle\) the average particle radius in the pore.  
The \(-\ln(1-\eta)\) term cancels in the difference \(\mu_1^{\rm ex}-\mu_2^{\rm ex}\), giving  

\[
\beta(\mu_1^{\rm ex}-\mu_2^{\rm ex})
   =\frac{3\eta}{1-\eta}\frac{R_1-R_2}{\langle R\rangle}
   +\frac{3\eta^{2}}{(1-\eta)^{2}}
     \frac{R_1^{2}-R_2^{2}}{\langle R\rangle^{2}} .
\tag{2}
\]

Using \(R_i=\sigma_i/2\) and \(\,R_1-R_2=-(\sigma_2-\sigma_1)/2\),  
\(R_1^{2}-R_2^{2}=-(\sigma_2^{2}-\sigma_1^{2})/4\), Eq. (2) becomes  

\[
-\beta(\mu_1^{\rm ex}-\mu_2^{\rm ex})
   =\frac{3\eta}{1-\eta}\,
     \frac{\sigma_2-\sigma_1}{2\langle R\rangle}
   +\frac{3\eta^{2}}{(1-\eta)^{2}}\,
     \frac{\sigma_2^{2}-\sigma_1^{2}}{4\langle R\rangle^{2}} .
\tag{3}
\]

Substituting (3) into (1) yields the high‑density selectivity  

\[
S_{12}^{\rm high}
   =\exp\!\Bigg[
      \frac{3\eta}{1-\eta}\,
      \frac{\sigma_2-\sigma_1}{2\langle R\rangle}
      +\frac{3\eta^{2}}{(1-\eta)^{2}}\,
      \frac{\sigma_2^{2}-\sigma_1^{2}}{4\langle R\rangle^{2}}
      \Bigg].
\tag{4}
\]

---

### Approximation for \(\langle R\rangle\)

If the composition in the pore is close to the bulk composition,
\(\langle R\rangle\approx y_1R_1+y_2R_2=
\frac{1}{2}\big(y_1\sigma_1+y_2\sigma_2\big)\equiv\frac{\sigma_{\rm av}}{2}\).
Inserting this into (4) gives the compact form

\[
\boxed{
S_{12}^{\rm high}
   \;\approx\;
   \exp\!\Bigg[
      \frac{3\eta}{1-\eta}\,
      \frac{\sigma_2-\sigma_1}{\sigma_{\rm av}}
      +\frac{3\eta^{2}}{(1-\eta)^{2}}\,
      \frac{\sigma_2^{2}-\sigma_1^{2}}{\sigma_{\rm av}^{2}}
      \Bigg]
   } ,
\qquad 
\sigma_{\rm av}=y_1\sigma_1+y_2\sigma_2 .
\tag{5}
\]

For an equimolar mixture (\(y_1=y_2=1/2\)) one has \(\sigma_{\rm av}= (\sigma_1+\sigma_2)/2\) and Eq. (5) simplifies further to

\[
\boxed{
S_{12}^{\rm high}
   \;\approx\;
   \exp\!\Bigg[
      \frac{6\eta(1+\eta)}{(1-\eta)^{2}}\,
      \frac{\sigma_2-\sigma_1}{\sigma_1+\sigma_2}
      \Bigg]
   } .
\tag{6}
\]

Equations (5)–(6) give the desired approximate expression for the adsorption selectivity in the high‑density (hard‑sphere) regime, expressed solely in terms of the packing fraction \(\eta\) and the particle diameters \(\sigma_1,\sigma_2\).  The exponent is positive because \(\sigma_2>\sigma_1\); consequently \(S_{12}^{\rm high}>1\), i.e. the smaller species (1) is preferentially adsorbed at high loadings.  The magnitude of the selectivity grows with increasing \(\eta\) and with increasing size disparity \((\sigma_2-\sigma_1)/(\sigma_1+\sigma_2)\).

r₍ads₎ = k₍ads₎ C₍PS₎ (1 − θ),   k₍ads₎ = A₍ads₎ exp(−E₍ads₎/(R T))

where C₍PS₎ is the bulk polysulfide concentration, θ the fractional surface coverage, E₍ads₎ = −ΔG₍ads₎ the adsorption activation energy, A₍ads₎ a pre‑exponential factor, R the gas constant and T the temperature.

2. Surface diffusion of the adsorbed polysulfide species to nucleation sites where they are reduced to solid Li₂S, characterized by a surface diffusion coefficient

D₍s₎ = A₍diff₎ exp(−E₍diff₎/(R T))

with E₍diff₎ the diffusion activation energy and A₍diff₎ a pre‑exponential factor. The flux of polysulfide to a nucleation site (assumed to be a circular sink of radius rₙ on each nanoparticle) under steady‑state conditions is approximated by

J₍diff₎ = (2π D₍s₎ θ) / ln(Rₚ / rₙ),

where Rₚ is the radius of the oxide nanoparticle (assumed much larger than rₙ).

The overall sulfide deposition efficiency η of a given oxide is defined as the ratio of the diffusion‑limited flux to the total rate at which polysulfide molecules arrive at the surface (adsorption + desorption). Assuming desorption follows the reverse of the adsorption step with rate constant k₍des₎ = A₍ads₎ exp(−E₍des₎/(R T)) where E₍des₎ = −ΔG₍ads₎ + λ (with λ = 0.05 eV accounting for an entropic penalty), the net arrival rate per unit area is

r₍net₎ = k₍ads₎ C₍PS₎ (1 − θ) − k₍des₎ θ.

At steady state, the surface coverage θ satisfies r₍net₎ = J₍diff₎.

You are given the following data for three candidate oxides (all evaluated at T = 350 K; R = 8.314×10⁻³ kJ mol⁻¹ K⁻¹; C₍PS₎ = 0.02 mol m⁻³; Rₚ = 20 nm; rₙ = 2 nm; A₍ads₎ = 1.0×10⁵ m³ mol⁻¹ s⁻¹; A₍diff₎ = 1.0×10⁻⁶ m² s⁻¹):

| Oxide | E₍ads₎ (eV) | E₍diff₎ (eV) |
|-------|--------------|---------------|
| MgO   | 0.45         | 0.30          |
| CeO₂  | 0.60         | 0.20          |
| La₂O₃ | 0.55         | 0.25          |

**Task**

The combined metric is  

\[
M(d)=A(d)\,G(d)=A_{\max}\,
\frac{\exp\!\Big[-\dfrac{(d-d_{0})^{2}}{2\sigma^{2}}\Big]}{d}\qquad 
\bigl(G(d)\propto 1/d\bigr)
\]

(we set the proportionality constant of \(G\) to 1, because it does not affect the optimum).

---

### Maximisation

\[
\frac{dM}{dd}=0\;\Longrightarrow\;
\frac{d}{dd}\Big[\frac{\exp\!\big[-(d-d_{0})^{2}/(2\sigma^{2})\big]}{d}\Big]=0
\]

Let  

\[
g(d)=\exp\!\Big[-\frac{(d-d_{0})^{2}}{2\sigma^{2}}\Big].
\]

Then  

\[
M(d)=\frac{g(d)}{d},\qquad 
\frac{dM}{dd}= \frac{d\,g'(d)-g(d)}{d^{2}}=0
\]

\[
\Longrightarrow\; \frac{g'(d)}{g(d)}=\frac{1}{d}.
\]

Because  

\[
\frac{g'(d)}{g(d)}=
-\frac{d-d_{0}}{\sigma^{2}},
\]

the condition becomes  

\[
-\frac{d-d_{0}}{\sigma^{2}}=\frac{1}{d}
\;\Longrightarrow\;
-d(d-d_{0})=\sigma^{2}
\]

\[
\Longrightarrow\; d^{2}-d_{0}d+\sigma^{2}=0 .
\]

Solving the quadratic gives  

\[
d=\frac{d_{0}\pm\sqrt{d_{0}^{2}-4\sigma^{2}}}{2}.
\]

With the given numbers  

\[
d_{0}=60\;\mu\text{m},\qquad \sigma=20\;\mu\text{m},
\]

\[
\sqrt{d_{0}^{2}-4\sigma^{2}}=\sqrt{60^{2}-4\cdot20^{2}}
=\sqrt{3600-1600}= \sqrt{2000}\approx 44.72\;\mu\text{m}.
\]

Hence  

\[
d_{1}= \frac{60+44.72}{2}=52.4\;\mu\text{m},\qquad
d_{2}= \frac{60-44.72}{2}=7.6\;\mu\text{m}.
\]

The experimental range is \(10\;\mu\text{m}\le d\le150\;\mu\text{m}\); therefore the admissible optimum is  

\[
\boxed{d_{\text{opt}}\approx 52\;\mu\text{m}} .
\]

### Value of the metric at the optimum

\[
M_{\max}=A_{\max}\,\frac{\exp\!\big[-(d_{\text{opt}}-d_{0})^{2}/(2\sigma^{2})\big]}
{d_{\text{opt}}}.
\]

\[
d_{\text{opt}}-d_{0}=52.4-60=-7.6\;\mu\text{m},
\qquad (d_{\text{opt}}-d_{0})^{2}=58.3\;\mu\text{m}^{2}.
\]

\[
\exp\!\Big[-\frac{58.3}{2\cdot20^{2}}\Big]
=\exp\!\Big[-\frac{58.3}{800}\Big]
=\exp(-0.0729)\approx 0.93 .
\]

Thus  

\[
M_{\max}=0.95\times\frac{0.93}{52.4}
\approx\frac{0.8835}{52.4}
\approx 1.7\times10^{-2}\;\text{(arbitrary units)}.
\]

\[
\boxed{M_{\max}\approx 1.7\times10^{-2}\ \text{(a.u.)}}.
\]

Hence, the fiber spacing that best balances cell alignment and electrical conductance is about **52 µm**, giving a maximal combined metric of roughly **0.017 (arbitrary units)**.

\[

N(t)=N_{0}\,e^{-k_{d}t},

\[

\]

\[

\]

The Cu‑site balance for the CO‑adsorbing sites is  

\[
[{\rm Cu(I)}]_{\rm free}+[{\rm Cu(I)}\!-\!{\rm CO}]
        = N_{\rm Cu(I)}. \tag{1}
\]

*Oxygen‑vacancy sites* – The areal density of oxygen vacancies is \(V_{O}\) (mol g\(^{-1}\)).  
They are the only sites that can bind O\(_2\). The vacancy‑site balance is  

\[
[ V_{O}]_{\rm free}+ [V_{O}{\!-\!}{\rm O}_{2}]
        = V_{O}. \tag{2}
\]

\[
K_{\rm CO}= \frac{[{\rm Cu(I)}\!-\!{\rm CO}]}{[{\rm Cu(I)}]_{\rm free}\;P_{\rm CO}},
\qquad
K_{O_{2}}= \frac{[V_{O}{\!-\!}{\rm O}_{2}]}{[ V_{O}]_{\rm free}\;P_{O_{2}}}.
\tag{3}
\]

Define the fractional coverages  

\[
\theta_{\rm CO}= \frac{[{\rm Cu(I)}\!-\!{\rm CO}]}{N_{\rm Cu(I)}},
\qquad
\theta_{O_{2}}= \frac{[V_{O}{\!-\!}{\rm O}_{2}]}{V_{O}}.
\]

Using (1)–(3) one obtains the usual Langmuir expressions  

\[
\theta_{\rm CO}= \frac{K_{\rm CO}\,P_{\rm CO}}{1+K_{\rm CO}\,P_{\rm CO}},\qquad
\theta_{O_{2}}= \frac{K_{O_{2}}\,P_{O_{2}}}{1+K_{O_{2}}\,P_{O_{2}}}. \tag{4}
\]

3. **Rate‑determining step**

The surface reaction  

\[
{\rm Cu(I)}\!-\!{\rm CO}+V_{O}{\!-\!}{\rm O}_{2}
\;\xrightarrow{k}\;
{\rm Cu(I)}+V_{O}+{\rm CO}_{2}
\]

is taken as the elementary step that controls the overall rate.  
Hence the rate of CO\(_2\) formation per gram of catalyst is  

\[
r = k\,[{\rm Cu(I)}\!-\!{\rm CO}]\,[V_{O}{\!-\!}{\rm O}_{2}]
   = k\,\big(N_{\rm Cu(I)}\theta_{\rm CO}\big)\,\big(V_{O}\theta_{O_{2}}\big). \tag{5}
\]

Insert (4) into (5) and use the definition of \(N_{\rm Cu(I)}\):

\[
\begin{aligned}
r &= k\;C_{\rm Cu}\,f_{1}\,(1-\theta_{\rm OH})\;V_{O}\;
      \frac{K_{\rm CO}\,P_{\rm CO}}{1+K_{\rm CO}\,P_{\rm CO}}\;
      \frac{K_{O_{2}}\,P_{O_{2}}}{1+K_{O_{2}}\,P_{O_{2}}}.
\end{aligned}
\tag{6}
\]

5. **Temperature dependence of the elementary rate constant**

The Arrhenius expression for the intrinsic rate constant of the RDS is  

\[
k = k_{0}\,\exp\!\Big(-\frac{E_{a}}{RT}\Big). \tag{7}
\]

Combining (6) and (7) gives the final rate law for CO oxidation on the Cu/TiO\(_2\) catalyst:

\[

r \;=\;
k_{0}\,\exp\!\Big(-\frac{E_{a}}{RT}\Big)\;
C_{\rm Cu}\,f_{1}\,(1-\theta_{\rm OH})\,V_{O}\;
\frac{K_{\rm CO}\,P_{\rm CO}}{1+K_{\rm CO}\,P_{\rm CO}}\;
\frac{K_{O_{2}}\,P_{O_{2}}}{1+K_{O_{2}}\,P_{O_{2}}}
}
\qquad\big[\text{mol CO}_{2}\,\text{g}^{-1}\,\text{s}^{-1}\big].
\]

**Site‑balance assumptions used**

* The total Cu sites are fixed at \(C_{\rm Cu}\); only the fraction \(f_{1}\) (Cu(I)) can bind CO.  
* Hydroxyl groups block a fraction \(\theta_{\rm OH}\) of *all* Cu sites, removing them from the Cu(I) pool.

* The surface reaction between adsorbed CO and O\(_2\) is the sole rate‑determining step; desorption of CO\(_2\) is fast.  

In the low‑pressure limit \((K_{\rm CO}P_{\rm CO}\ll1,\;K_{O_{2}}P_{O_{2}}\ll1)\) the expression reduces to  

\[
r \approx k_{0}\,e^{-E_{a}/RT}\;
C_{\rm Cu}\,f_{1}\,(1-\theta_{\rm OH})\,V_{O}\;
K_{\rm CO}K_{O_{2}}\;P_{\rm CO}\,P_{O_{2}},

The adsorption equilibrium constant follows from the standard free energy of adsorption  

\[
K_{\rm ads}(T)=\exp\!\Big[-\frac{\Delta G_{\rm ads}}{RT}\Big]\qquad(\Delta G_{\rm ads}={\rm const}).
\]

Hence, for a fixed bulk Na⁺ concentration \(c\) the surface coverage given by the Stern adsorption isotherm is  

\[
\boxed{\displaystyle 
\theta(T)=\frac{K_{\rm ads}(T)\,c}{1+K_{\rm ads}(T)\,c}
      =\frac{c\,\exp\!\big[-\Delta G_{\rm ads}/(RT)\big]}
             {1+c\,\exp\!\big[-\Delta G_{\rm ads}/(RT)\big]}} .
\tag{1}
\]

---

### Temperature derivative of \(\theta\)

\[
\frac{{\rm d}K_{\rm ads}}{{\rm d}T}
   =K_{\rm ads}\,\frac{\Delta G_{\rm ads}}{R\,T^{2}},
\qquad
\frac{{\rm d}\theta}{{\rm d}K_{\rm ads}}
   =\frac{c}{\bigl(1+K_{\rm ads}c\bigr)^{2}} .
\]

Therefore  

\[
\boxed{\displaystyle 
\frac{{\rm d}\theta}{{\rm d}T}
   =\frac{c\,K_{\rm ads}\,\Delta G_{\rm ads}}
          {R\,T^{2}\,\bigl(1+K_{\rm ads}c\bigr)^{2}}
   =\frac{c\,\Delta G_{\rm ads}}
          {R\,T^{2}}\,
     \frac{\exp[-\Delta G_{\rm ads}/(RT)]}
          {\bigl[1+c\,\exp[-\Delta G_{\rm ads}/(RT)]\bigr]^{2}} } .
\tag{2}
\]

Because adsorption is exergonic (\(\Delta G_{\rm ads}<0\)), the factor \(\Delta G_{\rm ads}/(R T^{2})\) is negative; consequently \({\rm d}\theta/{\rm d}T<0\).  **Increasing the temperature reduces the fraction of surfactant charge neutralised by adsorbed Na⁺ ions.**

---

### Stern‑layer contribution to the surface potential

The net surface charge density after partial neutralisation is  

\[
\sigma = -\frac{e}{A}\bigl(1-\theta\bigr) ,
\]

where \(e\) is the elementary charge and \(A\) the molecular area.  
The Stern layer behaves as a parallel‑plate capacitor with capacitance per unit area  

\[
C_{S}= \frac{\varepsilon_{0}\varepsilon_{r}}{d}.
\]

Hence the potential drop across the Stern layer is  

\[
\Delta V_{S}= \frac{\sigma}{C_{S}}
           = -\frac{e}{A\,C_{S}}\bigl(1-\theta\bigr)
           = -\frac{e}{A\,C_{S}}\,
              \frac{1}{1+K_{\rm ads}c}.
\]

Substituting the temperature‑dependent \(K_{\rm ads}\) gives the explicit temperature dependence  

\[
\boxed{\displaystyle 
\Delta V_{S}(T)=
-\frac{e}{A\,C_{S}}\,
\frac{1}
     {1+c\,\exp\!\big[-\Delta G_{\rm ads}/(RT)\big]} } .
\tag{3}
\]

Differentiating (3) with respect to \(T\) and using (2) yields  

\[
\boxed{\displaystyle 
\frac{{\rm d}\Delta V_{S}}{{\rm d}T}
   =\frac{e}{A\,C_{S}}\,
     \frac{{\rm d}\theta}{{\rm d}T}
   =\frac{e\,c\,\Delta G_{\rm ads}}
          {A\,C_{S}\,R\,T^{2}}\,
     \frac{\exp[-\Delta G_{\rm ads}/(RT)]}
          {\bigl[1+c\,\exp[-\Delta G_{\rm ads}/(RT)]\bigr]^{2}} } .
\tag{4}
\]

Because \(\Delta G_{\rm ads}<0\), \({\rm d}\Delta V_{S}/{\rm d}T<0\); the Stern‑layer potential becomes **more negative (or less positive)** as the temperature is raised.  

Thus a temperature‑independent standard free energy of adsorption leads to a temperature‑dependent equilibrium constant, which reduces the surface coverage \(\theta\) with increasing \(T\) and, through the Stern capacitance, makes the Stern contribution to the total surface potential \(\Delta V\) increasingly negative.

For a first‑order reaction the rate law is  

\[
r=-\frac{dC}{dt}=k\,C ,
\]

where the rate constant follows the Arrhenius law  

\[
k=A\,\exp\!\Big(-\frac{E_a}{RT}\Big) .
\]

The turnover frequency (TOF) is defined as the number of reactant molecules (or moles) that react per active site per unit time.  If the concentration of reactant that each active site “sees’’ is taken as the bulk concentration \(C\) (or, equivalently, if we normalize the concentration to one mole of site), the rate per site is simply the rate constant:

\[
\text{TOF}= \frac{r}{N_{\text{sites}}}=k .
\]

Hence, for a first‑order catalytic reaction the TOF depends only on the Arrhenius parameters:

\[
\boxed{\displaystyle \text{TOF}(T)=A\,\exp\!\Big(-\frac{E_a}{RT}\Big)}\qquad\text{[s}^{-1}\text{]}
\]

where  

- \(A\) = pre‑exponential factor (s\(^{-1}\)),  
- \(E_a\) = apparent activation energy (J mol\(^{-1}\)),  
- \(R = 8.314\;\text{J mol}^{-1}\text{K}^{-1}\), and  
- \(T\) = absolute temperature (K).

- Building block A consists of a central benzene core bearing three aldehyde groups at 120° and six peripheral phenyl rings attached to the core. Each peripheral phenyl can be substituted with 0, 1, or 2 fluorine atoms (all ortho to the bond to the core).
- The diamine D is a simple 1,4‑phenylenediamine.

q(P) = (q₁ b₁ P)/(1 + b₁ P) + (q₂ b₂ P)/(1 + b₂ P)

where q₁ = 0.5 mmol g⁻¹, q₂ = 0.3 mmol g⁻¹ for all COFs, but the affinity constants b₁ and b₂ depend on the fluorination level via the relation

ln bᵢ = αᵢ + βᵢ × (n_F/12)

with n_F the total number of fluorine atoms per monomer (0, 6, 12). The parameters are: α₁ = 5.0, β₁ = –1.5; α₂ = 4.2, β₂ = –1.0.

ln b_i = α_i + β_i * (n_F / 12)

with i = 1,2.

**Derivation**

For the four elementary steps the elementary rates per gram of catalyst are  

\[
\begin{aligned}
r_{a1}&=k_{a1}\,p_{NH_3}\,\theta_S , &
r_{d1}&=k_{d1}\,\theta_{S\!-\!NH_3},\\[2mm]
r_{m}&=k_{m}\,\theta_{S\!-\!NH_3}\,\theta_{Fe}, &
r_{-m}&=k_{-m}\,\theta_{Fe\!-\!NH_3}\,\theta_S ,\\[2mm]
r_{r}&=k_{r}\,\theta_{Fe\!-\!NH_3}\,p_{NO}\,p_{O_2}^{1/2}\qquad(\text{RDS})
\end{aligned}
\]

The coverages obey the site balances  

\[
\theta_S+\theta_{S\!-\!NH_3}=1 ,\qquad 
\theta_{Fe}+\theta_{Fe\!-\!NH_3}=1 .
\]

---

### 1.  Quasi‑steady state for the adsorbed intermediates  

\[
\begin{aligned}
\frac{d\theta_{S\!-\!NH_3}}{dt}=0&\;:\;
k_{a1}p_{NH_3}\theta_S
      =k_{d1}\theta_{S\!-\!NH_3}
      +k_{m}\theta_{S\!-\!NH_3}\theta_{Fe}
      -k_{-m}\theta_{Fe\!-\!NH_3}\theta_S \tag{1}\\[2mm]
\frac{d\theta_{Fe\!-\!NH_3}}{dt}=0&\;:\;
k_{m}\theta_{S\!-\!NH_3}\theta_{Fe}
      =k_{-m}\theta_{Fe\!-\!NH_3}\theta_S
      +k_{r}\theta_{Fe\!-\!NH_3}p_{NO}p_{O_2}^{1/2}\tag{2}
\end{aligned}
\]

Add (1) and (2) to eliminate the migration terms:

\[
k_{a1}p_{NH_3}\theta_S
   =k_{d1}\theta_{S\!-\!NH_3}
   +k_{r}\theta_{Fe\!-\!NH_3}p_{NO}p_{O_2}^{1/2}. \tag{3}
\]

---

### 2.  Equilibrium of the fast steps  

Because step 3 is rate‑determining, the reversible steps 1 and 2 are fast and can be taken at (quasi‑)equilibrium:

\[
\boxed{ \theta_{S\!-\!NH_3}=K_{NH_3}\,\theta_S\,p_{NH_3}},\qquad 
K_{NH_3}\equiv\frac{k_{a1}}{k_{d1}} \tag{4}
\]

\[
\boxed{ \theta_{Fe\!-\!NH_3}=K_m\,
        \frac{\theta_{S\!-\!NH_3}\,\theta_{Fe}}{\theta_S}},\qquad 
K_m\equiv\frac{k_m}{k_{-m}} . \tag{5}
\]

Insert (4) into (5) and use the Fe‑site balance \(\theta_{Fe}=1-\theta_{Fe\!-\!NH_3}\):

\[
\theta_{Fe\!-\!NH_3}
   =\frac{K_m K_{NH_3}p_{NH_3}\,\theta_{Fe}}
          {1+K_{NH_3}p_{NH_3}} . \tag{6}
\]

Now write the Fe‑site balance \(\theta_{Fe}=1-\theta_{Fe\!-\!NH_3}\) and solve (6) for \(\theta_{Fe\!-\!NH_3}\):

\[
\theta_{Fe\!-\!NH_3}
   =\frac{K_{NH_3}K_m\,p_{NH_3}}
          {1+K_{NH_3}p_{NH_3}+K_{NH_3}K_m\,p_{NH_3}} . \tag{7}
\]

Define the **overall effective adsorption constant**

\[
\boxed{K_{\text{eff}}\equiv K_{NH_3}K_m
      =\frac{k_{a1}\,k_m}{k_{d1}\,k_{-m}} } .
\]

Then (7) becomes

\[
\theta_{Fe\!-\!NH_3}= \frac{K_{\text{eff}}\,p_{NH_3}}
                         {1+K_{NH_3}p_{NH_3}+K_{\text{eff}}p_{NH_3}} . \tag{8}
\]

---

### 3.  Overall rate

The rate of the rate‑determining surface reaction per gram of catalyst is

\[
r = N_{Fe}\,k_{r}\,\theta_{Fe\!-\!NH_3}\,
    p_{NO}\,p_{O_2}^{1/2}.
\]

Substituting (8) gives the desired rate law

\[
\boxed{ \displaystyle 
r = \frac{ N_{Fe}\,k_{r}\,K_{\text{eff}}\,
          p_{NH_3}\,p_{NO}\,p_{O_2}^{1/2} }
         { 1 + K_{NH_3}\,p_{NH_3} + K_{\text{eff}}\,p_{NH_3} } } .
\]

---

**Composite constants**

\[
\boxed{ K_{NH_3}= \frac{k_{a1}}{k_{d1}} } ,\qquad
\boxed{ K_{\text{eff}}= \frac{k_{a1}\,k_{m}}{k_{d1}\,k_{-m}}
      = K_{NH_3}\,\frac{k_{m}}{k_{-m}} } .
\]

These definitions together with the expression above give the explicit NH₃‑SCR rate in terms of the gas‑phase partial pressures, site densities and kinetic parameters.

| Catalyst (Si/Al) | Time (h) | Epoxide conversion, X | Selectivity to D, S_D | Selectivity to K, S_K | Selectivity to O, S_O |

| H‑ZSM‑5 (23)    | 3        | 0.49                 | 0.52                  | 0.30                  | 0.18                  |

The intrinsic first‑order rate constants for the three parallel pathways are proportional to the initial site concentration:

\[
k_i = \beta\,C_{A0}\,\gamma_i
      = \beta\Bigl(\frac{\alpha}{R}\Bigr)\gamma_i
      =\frac{\alpha\beta\,\gamma_i}{R},
\qquad i\in\{D,K,O\}.
\]

Define  

\[
k_{\rm tot}=k_D+k_K+k_O
           =\frac{\alpha\beta}{R}\bigl(\gamma_D+\gamma_K+\gamma_O\bigr),
\]
\[
k_{\rm side}=k_K+k_O
            =\frac{\alpha\beta}{R}\bigl(\gamma_K+\gamma_O\bigr).
\]

Deactivation is first‑order in the active‑site concentration with a rate constant that depends on the instantaneous side‑reaction rate:

\[
k_d = \delta\,(k_K+k_O)\,C_E
     = \delta\,k_{\rm side}\,C_E .
\]

\[
\boxed{\;
\frac{dC_E}{dt}= -\,k_{\rm tot}\,C_E\,C_A
               = -\,\frac{\alpha\beta}{R}\,
                  \bigl(\gamma_D+\gamma_K+\gamma_O\bigr)\,
                  C_E\,C_A\;},
\]

\[
\boxed{\;
\frac{dC_A}{dt}= -\,k_d\,C_A
               = -\,\delta\,k_{\rm side}\,C_E\,C_A
               = -\,\delta\,\frac{\alpha\beta}{R}\,
                  \bigl(\gamma_K+\gamma_O\bigr)\,
                  C_E\,C_A\;}.
\]

with the initial conditions  

\[
C_E(0)=C_{E0}\quad(\text{feed concentration}),\qquad 
C_A(0)=\frac{\alpha}{R}.
\]

These equations fully describe the time evolution of epoxide conversion and catalyst deactivation for any zeolite characterized by its Si/Al ratio R.

\[

\[

\]

\[
\int_{0}^{\infty}r^{\nu-1}J_{0}(kr)\,dr = k^{-\nu}\,\frac{\Gamma(\nu)}{2^{\nu-1}}
\qquad(\Re \nu>0),
\]

to \(\nu=-4\) gives  

\[
\int_{0}^{\infty}r^{-5}J_{0}(kr)\,dr=-\frac{1}{2}\,k^{4}.
\]

Hence  

\[
\widehat{V}_{\rm vdW}(k)=2\pi(-A)\Bigl(-\frac12\,k^{4}\Bigr)
                        =-\pi A\,k^{2}.
\]

---

### 2.  Screened electrostatic part  

The 2‑D screened Coulomb kernel can be written as the modified Bessel function  
\(K_{0}(\kappa r)\); it has the well‑known transform  

\[
\int_{0}^{\infty}r\,J_{0}(kr)\,K_{0}(\kappa r)\,dr=\frac{1}{k^{2}+\kappa^{2}} .

The Lennard–Jones interaction between the probe centre and a carbon atom is  

\[
U_{i}(d)=4\varepsilon\Big[\Big(\frac{\sigma}{d}\Big)^{12}-\Big(\frac{\sigma}{d}\Big)^{6}\Big],
\qquad d\equiv\big\|\mathbf r-\mathbf R_i\big\| .
\]

If we replace the soft LJ repulsion by a hard‑sphere exclusion radius \(r_{\text{ex}}\), the probe centre is allowed at a point \(\mathbf r\) only when the total energy does not exceed the prescribed threshold \(U_{\text{thr}}\).  Assuming that the contribution from the nearest carbon atom dominates the sum, we require  

\[
U_{i}\big(d_{\min}\big)\;\le\;U_{\text{thr}},
\qquad 
d_{\min}(\mathbf r)=\min_{i}\big\|\mathbf r-\mathbf R_i\big\|_{\text{PBC}} .
\]

Setting the equality \(U_{i}(d_{\min})=U_{\text{thr}}\) defines the exclusion distance:

\[
4\varepsilon\Big[\Big(\frac{\sigma}{d_{\min}}\Big)^{12}
-\Big(\frac{\sigma}{d_{\min}}\Big)^{6}\Big]=U_{\text{thr}} .
\]

Introduce \(y\equiv (\sigma/d_{\min})^{6}\); then  

\[
4\varepsilon\,(y^{2}-y)=U_{\text{thr}}
\;\Longrightarrow\;
y^{2}-y-\frac{U_{\text{thr}}}{4\varepsilon}=0 .
\]

Solving the quadratic for the positive root gives  

\[
y=\frac{1+\sqrt{\,1+U_{\text{thr}}/\varepsilon\,}}{2}.
\]

Since \(y=(\sigma/d_{\min})^{6}\),

\[
d_{\min}= \sigma\,y^{-1/6}
          =\sigma\Bigg[\frac{2}{1+\sqrt{1+U_{\text{thr}}/\varepsilon}}\Bigg]^{1/6}.
\]

The distance \(d_{\min}\) is the hard‑sphere exclusion radius for the probe centre; it implicitly contains the probe radius \(r_{p}\) because the Lennard–Jones parameters \(\sigma\) and \(\varepsilon\) are the mixed (e.g. Lorentz–Berthelot) parameters for the carbon–probe pair, i.e.  

\[
\sigma_{\text{eff}} = r_{p}+r_{C}^{\text{vdW}},\qquad
\varepsilon_{\text{eff}} =\sqrt{\varepsilon_{C}\,\varepsilon_{p}} .
\]

Hence we define  

\[
r_{\text{ex}}(r_{p},\varepsilon,\sigma,U_{\text{thr}})
   =\sigma_{\text{eff}}\Bigg[\frac{2}
   {1+\sqrt{1+U_{\text{thr}}/\varepsilon_{\text{eff}}}}\Bigg]^{1/6}.
\]

### Accessibility criterion for a grid point  

A grid point \(\mathbf r_{g}\) is **accessible** if the shortest distance to any carbon atom (including periodic images) exceeds the exclusion radius:

\[
\boxed{\;
\min_{i}\big\|\mathbf r_{g}-\mathbf R_{i}\big\|_{\text{PBC}}
\;\ge\; r_{\text{ex}}(r_{p},\varepsilon,\sigma,U_{\text{thr}})
\;}
\]

If the inequality is violated, the point is excluded from the pore‑volume count. This simple distance‑check replaces the explicit evaluation of the full Lennard‑Jones sum in the grid‑based algorithm.

The discretisation error comes from the “stair‑case’’ approximation of the surface that separates the accessible and the excluded region.  
For a smooth surface of total area \(S\) the volume error of a cubic grid of spacing \(\Delta\) is bounded by the volume of a thin shell of thickness \(\Delta\),

\[
\varepsilon_V \;\le\; S\,\Delta .
\]

The excluded region around each carbon atom can be approximated by a sphere of radius  

\[
r_{\rm ex}\;:\qquad 
U_i(r_{\rm ex})=U_{\rm thr}\;\;\Longrightarrow\;\;r_{\rm ex}=d\;(U_{\rm thr},\varepsilon,\sigma).
\]

For a single sphere  

\[
S=4\pi r_{\rm ex}^{2},\qquad 
V_{\rm ex}= \frac{4}{3}\pi r_{\rm ex}^{3},
\]

so that the relative error in the excluded (and therefore in the accessible) volume satisfies  

\[
\frac{\varepsilon_V}{V_{\rm ex}} \;\le\; \frac{S\,\Delta}{V_{\rm ex}}
      =\frac{4\pi r_{\rm ex}^{2}\,\Delta}{\frac{4}{3}\pi r_{\rm ex}^{3}}
      =\frac{3\,\Delta}{r_{\rm ex}} .
\]

Requiring this relative error to be smaller than the prescribed tolerance \(\eta\),

\[
\frac{3\,\Delta}{r_{\rm ex}}\;\le\;\eta
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\boxed{\;\Delta \;=\; \frac{\eta}{3}\;r_{\rm ex}\;}
\]

(and one may optionally include a safety factor \(0<\alpha\le1\) and use \(\Delta=\alpha\,\eta\,r_{\rm ex}/3\)).  

**Algorithmic prescription**

1. **Determine the exclusion radius**  
   Solve \(4\varepsilon[(\sigma/r_{\rm ex})^{12}-(\sigma/r_{\rm ex})^{6}]=U_{\rm thr}\) for \(r_{\rm ex}\).

2. **Choose the grid spacing**  
   Set \(\Delta = (\eta/3)\,r_{\rm ex}\).  

3. **Generate the cubic grid**  
   Number of points per direction: \(N_{\rm g}= \lceil L/\Delta\rceil\).  
   Grid points: \(\mathbf{r}_{ijk}= (i\Delta,\;j\Delta,\;k\Delta)\) with \(i,j,k=0,\dots,N_{\rm g}-1\) (periodic images are handled by the minimum‑image convention).

4. **Evaluate the total LJ energy** \(U_{\rm tot}(\mathbf{r}_{ijk})\) at each grid point, count the points that satisfy \(U_{\rm tot}\le U_{\rm thr}\), and compute  

   \[
   V_{\rm acc}= N_{\rm acc}\,\Delta^{3}.
   \]

With the choice \(\Delta = (\eta/3) r_{\rm ex}\) the discretisation error in the computed accessible volume is guaranteed to be below the relative tolerance \(\eta\).

\tag{2}
\]

\[

\tag{3}
\]

explicitly for the threshold condition).

---

### 2.  Kinetic energy on the excited surface at the crossing

\[
E_{\rm tot}=K(z)+V_{e}(z)+V_{\rm im}(z) .
\tag{4}
\]

Evaluating (4) at the crossing point and using (1) gives the kinetic energy there,

\[
K_{c}= \hbar\omega - V_{e}(z_{c})-V_{\rm im}(z_{c}) .
\tag{5}
\]

Because of the crossing condition (2), \(V_{e}(z_{c})=V_{g}(z_{c})\).

---

### 3.  Desorption condition (MGR mechanism)

\[

\tag{6}
\]

\tag{7}
\]

\[

\]

\[

is the minimum photon energy required to induce desorption of neutral CO via the
Menzel‑Gomer‑Redhead mechanism.  (The Landau–Zener probability \(P_{\rm LZ}\) governs the
probability of the non‑adiabatic transition but does not alter the energetic

\[
w'=\frac{W}{L}\;\;(\text{kg m}^{-1}) .

The gas enthalpy flow rate at position \(z\) is  

\[
\dot H_g(z)=\sum_i N_i(z)\,C_{p,i}\,T(z) .
\]

The catalyst enthalpy per unit length is  

\[
\dot H_{cat}(z)=w'\,C_{p,\text{cat}}\,T(z) .
\]

The net heat released by the reactions in the slice is  

\[
\dot Q_{rxn}= -\Big[ \Delta H_{R1}\,r_1(z)+\Delta H_{R2}\,r_2(z)\Big]\,w'\,dz
\]

where  

\[
r_1=k\,\frac{p_{CO}\,p_{H_2}^{2}}{1+K_{CO}p_{CO}+K_{CO_2}p_{CO_2}+K_{CH_3OH}p_{CH_3OH}},\qquad
r_2=k\,\frac{p_{CO_2}\,p_{H_2}^{3}}{1+K_{CO}p_{CO}+K_{CO_2}p_{CO_2}+K_{CH_3OH}p_{CH_3OH}} .
\]

Energy balance for the adiabatic slice (no external heat transfer) gives  

\[
\dot H_g(z) = \dot H_g(z+dz)+\dot H_{cat}(z+dz)-\dot H_{cat}(z)+\dot Q_{rxn}.
\]

Expanding to first order and neglecting higher‑order terms:

\[
\sum_i C_{p,i}\Big[T\,dN_i+N_i\,dT\Big] + w' C_{p,\text{cat}}\,dT
= -\Big[ \Delta H_{R1}\,r_1+\Delta H_{R2}\,r_2\Big]\,w'\,dz .
\]

\[
\Big(\sum_i N_i C_{p,i}+ w' C_{p,\text{cat}}\Big)\,dT
= -\Big[ \Delta H_{R1}\,r_1+\Delta H_{R2}\,r_2\Big]\,w'\,dz .
\]

Dividing by \(dz\) yields the differential temperature equation for the adiabatic packed‑bed:

\[
\boxed{%
\frac{dT}{dz}=-
\frac{w'\,\big[\,\Delta H_{R1}\,r_1(z)+\Delta H_{R2}\,r_2(z)\,\big]}
{\displaystyle\sum_i N_i(z)\,C_{p,i}+w'\,C_{p,\text{cat}}}
}
\]

with  

\[
r_1(z)=k\,\frac{p_{CO}\,p_{H_2}^{2}}{1+K_{CO}p_{CO}+K_{CO_2}p_{CO_2}+K_{CH_3OH}p_{CH_3OH}},\qquad
r_2(z)=k\,\frac{p_{CO_2}\,p_{H_2}^{3}}{1+K_{CO}p_{CO}+K_{CO_2}p_{CO_2}+K_{CH_3OH}p_{CH_3OH}} .
\]

b_A({\rm Na},H=0.8)&=10^{-5}\,e^{5.650}=2.85\times10^{-3}\ {\rm bar^{-1}}\\

\]

\[

\]

The diffusion time for a molecule to cross a characteristic length \(L\) can be obtained from Fick’s second law.  For a simple one‑dimensional (or isotropic) diffusion problem the characteristic time scale is

\[
\tau_D \;\sim\; \frac{L^{2}}{D_{\text{eff}}}\;,
\]

where \(D_{\text{eff}}\) is the effective diffusivity of the diffusing species in the medium.

---

### Application to a cubic MOF cage  

*Side length of the cage*  

\[
L = 2\ \text{nm}=2\times10^{-9}\ \text{m}
\]

\[
L^{2}= (2\times10^{-9}\ \text{m})^{2}=4\times10^{-18}\ \text{m}^{2}
\]

*Characteristic diffusion time*  

\[
\boxed{\displaystyle 
\tau_D = \frac{L^{2}}{D_{\text{eff}}}
        = \frac{4\times10^{-18}\ \text{m}^{2}}{D_{\text{eff}}\ (\text{m}^{2}\,\text{s}^{-1})}
        \;\text{s}
}
\]

---

### Numerical estimate (illustrative)

Typical effective diffusivities for small gases in microporous MOFs lie in the range  

\[
D_{\text{eff}}\;\approx\;10^{-9}\!-\!10^{-10}\ \text{m}^{2}\,\text{s}^{-1}.
\]

Using these values:

| \(D_{\text{eff}}\) (m² s⁻¹) | \(\tau_D\) (s) |
|---------------------------|----------------|
| \(1\times10^{-9}\)        | \(4\times10^{-9}\)  (≈ 4 ns) |
| \(1\times10^{-10}\)       | \(4\times10^{-8}\)  (≈ 40 ns) |

Thus, for a single 2 nm cage the diffusion of O₂ is essentially instantaneous (nanoseconds) compared with the experimentally observed induction period (seconds‑to‑minutes). 2. **Translational entropy loss** of the polymer upon adsorption.
3. **Steric repulsion** of the PEG side‑chains, modeled as a polymer brush in the Alexander–de Gennes regime.

\[

$$G_{s}^{0}(\varepsilon)=\frac{1}{\varepsilon-\Delta E-\Sigma_{s}(\varepsilon)}\,,\qquad \Sigma_{s}(\varepsilon)=\Delta w_{0}+\int_{-D}^{D}\frac{V^{2}\rho_{s}(\varepsilon')}{\varepsilon-\varepsilon'+i0^{+}}\,d\varepsilon' .$$

For comparison, a commercial supported catalyst **Catalyst C** (Ni/SiO₂‑Al₂O₃, Ni loading 10 wt %) is also studied. All three catalysts are evaluated for (i) NO decomposition (2 NO → N₂ + O₂) at 673 K and (ii) Fischer–Tropsch synthesis (FTS) at 523 K and 20 bar using a H₂/CO = 2 feed.

The following physicochemical data are available (all values are per gram of catalyst):

| Property | Catalyst A | Catalyst B | Catalyst C |
|----------|-----------|-----------|-----------|
| BET surface area, S<sub>BET</sub> (m² g⁻¹) | 120 | 115 | 150 |
| CO chemisorption uptake, θ<sub>CO</sub> (mmol g⁻¹) | 0.45 | 0.48 | 0.30 |
| CO chemisorption stoichiometry, ν (CO per surface Ni atom) | 1.0 | 1.0 | 1.0 |
| Average crystallite size from XRD, d (nm) | 12 | 10 | 25 |
| Metal‑support interaction factor, α (dimensionless, 0 < α ≤ 1) derived from in‑situ XRD (α = 1 for no interaction, lower values indicate stronger interaction) | 0.45 | 0.40 | 0.85 |

**Reaction testing conditions**

1. **NO decomposition**
   - Feed: 1 % NO in He, total flow = 100 cm³ min⁻¹ (STP).
   - Catalyst mass = 0.200 g, diluted with inert quartz to avoid channeling.
   - Measured steady‑state NO conversion, X<sub>NO</sub>:
     - A: 45 %
     - B: 48 %
     - C: 8 %

2. **Fischer–Tropsch synthesis**
   - Feed: H₂/CO = 2 (molar), total flow = 200 cm³ min⁻¹ (STP).
   - Catalyst mass = 0.150 g, same dilution protocol.
   - Measured steady‑state CO conversion, X<sub>CO</sub>:
     - A: 22 % (product distribution: CH₄ = 55 %, C₂‑C₄ = 30 % (alkenes), C₅⁺ = 15 %)
     - B: 24 % (product distribution: CH₄ = 50 %, C₂‑C₄ = 35 % (alkenes), C₅⁺ = 15 %)
     - C: 20 % (product distribution: CH₄ = 70 %, C₂‑C₄ = 0 % (no alkenes), C₅⁺ = 30 %).

Assume ideal gas behavior, and that the rate of reaction per catalyst mass follows a Langmuir–Hinshelwood (L‑H) expression of the form

\[ r = \frac{k\,P_i^{\,n}}{1 + \sum_j K_j P_j}, \]

where *k* is the intrinsic rate constant, *P* the partial pressure of the reacting species, *n* the reaction order with respect to the reactant *i*, and *K_j* the adsorption equilibrium constants for all surface‑adsorbed species *j*.

**Task 2a**: Derive an expression for the TOF (s⁻¹) for each reaction, defined as the number of reactant molecules converted per accessible active site per second.

The question is "Task 2a: Derive an expression for the TOF (s⁻¹) for each reaction, defined as the number of reactant molecules converted per accessible active site per second."

Thus we need to derive an expression for turnover frequency (TOF) for each reaction (NO decomposition and FTS) using given data. We need to express TOF in terms of measured conversion, flow rates, catalyst mass, and number of accessible active sites (determined from CO chemisorption uptake and stoichiometry). Also maybe include surface area and metal-support interaction factor? The problem may require a derivation that includes these variables.

Given the L-H expression r = (k P_i^n)/(1 + Σ K_j P_j). But for TOF, we need to relate reaction rate per mass to number of active sites. Usually TOF = r / (N_sites), where r is rate per mass (mol/s per gram) and N_sites is number of active sites per gram (mol/g). The number of active sites per gram can be estimated from CO chemisorption uptake: θ_CO (mmol/g) gives amount of CO adsorbed per gram, which is assumed to correspond to number of surface Ni atoms (active sites) times stoichiometry ν (CO per surface Ni atom). Since ν = 1, the number of surface Ni atoms per gram = θ_CO (mmol/g) = 0.45 mmol/g for A, 0.48 for B, 0.30 for C. However, we may need to adjust for metal-support interaction factor α: accessible active sites may be reduced by strong interaction (lower α). So effective active sites = α * θ_CO (mmol/g). Or perhaps the factor α indicates fraction of metal surface that is accessible (or fraction of Ni atoms that are available for reaction). So we can incorporate α.

Thus TOF = (Rate per gram) / (α * θ_CO * 10^-3 mol/g) [since θ_CO in mmol/g]. Rate per gram = (mol of reactant converted per second per gram). For NO decomposition: measured conversion X_NO = 45% for A, etc. The feed flow is 100 cm³/min at STP. At STP, 1 mol of gas occupies 22.414 L = 22414 cm³. So mol flow = Q / 22414 (cm³/min). For NO feed: 1% NO in He, so NO partial flow = 0.01 * Q. So mol NO flow = 0.01 * Q / 22414 (mol/min). Convert to mol/s by dividing by 60. Then conversion X_NO gives mol NO converted per minute = X_NO * (mol NO feed). So rate per gram = (X_NO * mol NO feed per minute) / (mass of catalyst). Then TOF = (rate per gram) / (α * θ_CO * 10^-3 mol/g). Units: s^-1.

Similarly for FTS: CO conversion X_CO = 22% etc. Feed flow 200 cm³/min total, with H2/CO=2. So the feed composition: ratio H2:CO = 2:1. So total moles per minute = Q/22414. Let fraction of CO in feed = 1/(1+2) = 1/3 (since total moles of gas = CO + 2H2 = 3 parts). So CO mol flow = (1/3)*Q/22414. Then conversion X_CO gives mol CO converted per minute = X_CO * CO mol flow. Rate per gram = that divided by catalyst mass (0.150 g). Then TOF = (rate per gram) / (α * θ_CO * 10^-3 mol/g). However, note that CO chemisorption measures Ni surface sites, but FTS may involve Ni sites as active for CO activation. The presence of Pt in catalyst B might also provide sites, but we assume Ni is the primary active site. So we use θ_CO as Ni sites.

Thus the derived expression for TOF for each reaction can be:

TOF = (X * Q * y_i / V_m) * (1/60) * (1/m_cat) / (α * θ_CO * 10^-3)

where X is conversion (fraction), Q is volumetric flow (cm³/min), y_i is mol fraction of reactant i in feed, V_m = 22414 cm³/mol at STP, m_cat is catalyst mass (g). Simplify:

TOF = \frac{X \, Q \, y_i}{V_m \, 60 \, m_{cat} \, \alpha \, \theta_{CO} \times 10^{-3}}

= \frac{X \, Q \, y_i}{V_m \, 60 \, m_{cat} \, \alpha \, \theta_{CO}} \times 10^3

But note that θ_CO is in mmol/g, so dividing by α*θ_CO (mmol/g) yields (mol/g) denominator: α * θ_CO * 10^-3 mol/g. So the factor 10^3 cancels? Let's check:

Rate per gram (mol/s/g) = (X * Q * y_i / V_m) * (1/60) / m_cat (g). Actually we…
answer:
\[
\boxed{\displaystyle 
\mathrm{TOF}_i \;=\;
\frac{X_i\,Q\,y_i}{V_m\,m_{\text{cat}}\,\alpha\,\theta_{\mathrm{CO}}}\;
\frac{10^{3}}{60}
\;\;(\text{s}^{-1})
}
\]

where  

* \(X_i\) = fractional conversion of reactant \(i\) (NO or CO),  
* \(Q\) = total volumetric flow (cm³ min⁻¹) at STP,  
* \(y_i\) = mole fraction of reactant \(i\) in the feed (\(y_{\mathrm{NO}}=0.01\), \(y_{\mathrm{CO}}=1/3\) for H₂/CO = 2),  
* \(V_m=22\,414\;\text{cm}^3\;\text{mol}^{-1}\) (molar volume at STP),  
* \(m_{\text{cat}}\) = catalyst mass (g) used in the test,  
* \(\alpha\) = metal‑support interaction factor,  
* \(\theta_{\mathrm{CO}}\) = CO chemisorption uptake (mmol g⁻¹) (ν = 1),  

and the factor \(10^{3}/60\) converts the rate from \(\text{mmol min}^{-1}\,\text{g}^{-1}\) to \(\text{mol s}^{-1}\,\text{g}^{-1}\) and then divides by the number of accessible active sites \((\alpha\,\theta_{\mathrm{CO}}\times10^{-3}\;\text{mol g}^{-1})\).  

Thus the same expression applies to NO decomposition (with \(y_{\mathrm{NO}}=0.01\)) and to Fischer–Tropsch synthesis (with \(y_{\mathrm{CO}}=1/3\)).

Consider a suspension of monodisperse spherical latex particles of radius a = 100 nm bearing an initial positive surface potential ψ₀ = +50 mV in aqueous solution at 25°C. An anionic polyelectrolyte (poly‑sodium‑styrene‑sulfonate, PSS) of molecular weight M (in kDa) is added at a bulk concentration Cₚ (mol L⁻¹). The polymer adsorbs onto the particle surface forming a layer of thickness

δ(M) = k₁ M^α nm,

where k₁ and α are constants, and the adsorbed amount per unit area Γ_{surf} follows a Langmuir isotherm

Γ_{surf} = \frac{Γ_{max}\,K(M)\,Cₚ}{1 + K(M)\,Cₚ}, \qquad K(M) = k₂\,M^β,

with Γ_{max} the maximum surface coverage (mol m⁻²) and k₂, β constants. Each monomer carries a charge –z e (z>0).

The effective surface potential after adsorption is approximated by a planar capacitor model

ψ_{eff} = ψ₀ - \frac{z e\,Γ_{surf}}{C_s}, \qquad C_s = \frac{εε₀}{λ_D},

where ε is the dielectric constant of water, ε₀ the vacuum permittivity, and λ_D the Debye length

λ_D = \left(\frac{εε₀ k_B T}{2 N_A e² I}\right)^{1/2},

I being the ionic strength of the solution.

The interaction potential between two identical particles at surface‑to‑surface separation h = r - 2a is described by DLVO theory:

V_{DLVO}(h) = V_{vdW}(h) + V_{EDL}(h),

with the van der Waals attraction

V_{vdW}(h) = -\frac{A_H}{12}\left[\frac{2a²}{h(2a+h)} + \frac{2a²}{(2a+h)²} + \ln\!\left(\frac{h}{2a+h}\right)\right],

and the double‑layer repulsion (for ψ_{eff} \ll k_B T/e)

V_{EDL}(h) = π ε ε₀ a ψ_{eff}²\,e^{-h/λ_D}.

In addition to DLVO forces, lateral heterogeneities (polymer “patches”) generate an attractive patch‑charge term

V_{patch}(h) = -π a² σ_p²\,e^{-h/λ_D}, \qquad σ_p = γ\,Γ_{surf},

where γ is a proportionality constant (C mol⁻¹ m⁻²).

**(a) Isoelectric point**
Derive an explicit expression for the polymer concentration Cₚ* that yields the isoelectric point (ψ_{eff}=0). Express Cₚ* in terms of M, I, and the parameters ψ₀, z, e, Γ_{max}, k₁, k₂, α, β.

A research team is developing a controlled‑release coating that incorporates an isothiazolinone biocide (2‑Octyl‑4‑isothiazolin‑3‑one, OIT) adsorbed onto three different inorganic mineral carriers: (i) a high‑surface‑area montmorillonite (MMT) with BET surface area 250 m² g⁻¹, average pore diameter 2 nm, and measured enthalpy of adsorption ΔHₐₚₚ = ‑45 kJ mol⁻¹; (ii) a low‑surface‑area kaolinite (KLT) with BET surface area 30 m² g⁻¹, average pore diameter 5 nm, ΔHₐₚₚ = ‑30 kJ mol⁻¹; and (iii) a synthetic zeolite (ZEO) with BET surface area 400 m² g⁻¹, average pore diameter 1 nm, ΔHₐₚₚ = ‑55 kJ mol⁻¹.

The biocide is introduced to the minerals by two processes: (A) a dry high‑shear milling (particle size reduction to a log‑normal distribution with D₅₀ = 0.8 µm) and (B) a wet impregnation (particle size unchanged, D₅₀ = 5 µm). After loading, the mineral–biocide composites are dispersed at 5 wt % in a water‑borne acrylic paint matrix. The final coating thickness is 100 µm, and the paint is assumed to be a non‑porous, homogeneous medium with diffusion coefficient for free OIT D₀ = 2 × 10⁻¹⁰ m² s⁻¹.

| Mineral | q_{\max} (mg g⁻¹) | K (L mg⁻¹) |
|---------|-------------------|------------|

Starting from the single‑site Langmuir isotherm  

\[
q=\frac{q_{\max}\,b(T)P}{1+b(T)P},
\]

solve for the affinity constant \(b(T)\):

\[
q\bigl[1+b(T)P\bigr]=q_{\max}b(T)P
\;\;\Longrightarrow\;\;
q=b(T)P\bigl(q_{\max}-q\bigr)
\;\;\Longrightarrow\;\;
b(T)=\frac{q}{P\,(q_{\max}-q)} .
\]

Take the natural logarithm and insert the van’t Hoff relation  

\[
\ln b(T)=\frac{\Delta S_{\rm ads}}{R}-\frac{\Delta H_{\rm ads}}{RT}.
\]

Hence  

\[
\boxed{\;
\ln\!\Bigl[\frac{q}{P\,(q_{\max}-q)}\Bigr]
= -\,\frac{\Delta H_{\rm ads}}{R}\,\frac{1}{T}
+ \frac{\Delta S_{\rm ads}}{R}\;}
\]

which is linear in \(1/T\).  

If one plots  

\[
y=\ln\!\Bigl[\frac{q}{P\,(q_{\max}-q)}\Bigr]
\quad\text{versus}\quad
x=\frac{1}{T},
\]

the slope equals \(-\Delta H_{\rm ads}/R\) and the intercept equals \(\Delta S_{\rm ads}/R\).  Simultaneous determination of \(\Delta H_{\rm ads}\) and \(\Delta S_{\rm ads}\) follows directly from the linear fit.

The Langmuir model for a 1 : 1 surface binding equilibrium is  

\[
\theta=\frac{K_{s}C}{1+K_{s}C}\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad 
\frac{\theta}{1-\theta}=K_{s}C .
\]

Thus a plot of  

\[
y\equiv\frac{\theta}{1-\theta}\;\; \text{vs.}\;\; x\equiv C
\]

should be a straight line through the origin whose slope is the surface
equilibrium constant \(K_{s}\).

---

### 1.  Transform the experimental data

| \(C\) (M) | \(\theta\) | \(y=\theta/(1-\theta)\) |
|-----------|-----------|--------------------------|
| \(1.0\times10^{-3}\) | 0.31 | \(0.31/(0.69)=0.4493\) |
| \(5.0\times10^{-3}\) | 0.71 | \(0.71/(0.29)=2.4483\) |
| \(1.0\times10^{-2}\) | 0.86 | \(0.86/(0.14)=6.1429\) |

---

### 2.  Linear regression through the origin  

For a line \(y=K_{s}x\) the least‑squares estimate of the slope is  

\[
K_{s}= \frac{\displaystyle\sum_{i}x_{i}y_{i}}
            {\displaystyle\sum_{i}x_{i}^{2}} .
\]

Calculate the required sums:

\[
\begin{aligned}
\sum x_{i}y_{i}&=
(1.0\times10^{-3})(0.4493)+
(5.0\times10^{-3})(2.4483)+
(1.0\times10^{-2})(6.1429)\\
&=0.0004493+0.0122415+0.0614286\\
&=0.0741194,\\[4pt]
\sum x_{i}^{2}&=
(1.0\times10^{-3})^{2}+(5.0\times10^{-3})^{2}+(1.0\times10^{-2})^{2}\\
&=1.0\times10^{-6}+2.5\times10^{-5}+1.0\times10^{-4}\\
&=1.26\times10^{-4}.
\end{aligned}
\]

Hence  

\[
K_{s}= \frac{0.0741194}{1.26\times10^{-4}}
      =5.89\times10^{2}\;\text{M}^{-1}.
\]

---

### 3.  Result  

\[
\boxed{K_{s}\approx5.9\times10^{2}\ \text{M}^{-1}}
\]

(Using the individual points gives \(K_{s}=449,\;490,\;614\;\text{M}^{-1}\); the
least‑squares fit above provides the best overall estimate.)

**Derivation**

1. **Equilibrium condition** – At the freezing temperature inside a pore the chemical potentials of liquid water (ℓ) and ice (i) are equal  

\[
\mu_\ell\!\bigl(T_f(r),P_\ell\bigr)=\mu_i\!\bigl(T_f(r),P_i\bigr) .
\]

2. **Pressure jump across a curved interface** – For a cylindrical pore the ice–water interface has one finite principal radius equal to the pore radius \(r\) and the other infinite (along the pore axis).  With an isotropic interfacial tension \(\gamma_{wi}\) the Laplace pressure is  

\[
\Delta P\equiv P_\ell-P_i=\frac{\gamma_{wi}}{r}\; .
\]

3. **Expansion of the chemical potentials** – Expand each chemical potential about the bulk melting point \((T_f^{\rm bulk},P^{\rm bulk})\) where \(\mu_\ell^{\rm bulk}=\mu_i^{\rm bulk}\).  Using  

\[
\left(\frac{\partial\mu}{\partial T}\right)_P=-S,\qquad 
\left(\frac{\partial\mu}{\partial P}\right)_T=V_m ,
\]

and assuming the molar volume of liquid water \(V_{m,1}\) is constant, we obtain  

\[
\mu_\ell\approx\mu_\ell^{\rm bulk}
- S_\ell\,(T_f(r)-T_f^{\rm bulk})
+ V_{m,1}\,\Delta P,
\]

\[
\mu_i\approx\mu_i^{\rm bulk}
- S_i\,(T_f(r)-T_f^{\rm bulk}) .
\]

4. **Use \(\mu_\ell^{\rm bulk}=\mu_i^{\rm bulk}\)** and set the two expanded expressions equal:

\[
- S_\ell\Delta T + V_{m,1}\Delta P = - S_i\Delta T ,
\qquad \Delta T\equiv T_f(r)-T_f^{\rm bulk}.
\]

5. **Introduce the entropy of fusion** – The entropy change on melting per mole is  

\[
\Delta S_f = S_\ell - S_i = \frac{\Delta H_{f,1}}{T_f^{\rm bulk}} .
\]

Hence  

\[
(S_i - S_\ell)\Delta T = -\Delta S_f\,\Delta T = V_{m,1}\Delta P .
\]

6. **Solve for the temperature shift**  

\[
\Delta T = -\,\frac{V_{m,1}\,\Delta P\,T_f^{\rm bulk}}{\Delta H_{f,1}} .
\]

Because \(\Delta T\) is negative (the confined water freezes at a lower temperature), the freezing‑point depression is  

\[
\Delta T_f(r) \equiv T_f^{\rm bulk}-T_f(r)= -\Delta T
= \frac{V_{m,1}\,\Delta P\,T_f^{\rm bulk}}{\Delta H_{f,1}} .
\]

7. **Insert the Laplace pressure for a cylinder**  

\[
\Delta P = \frac{\gamma_{wi}}{r} .
\]

Finally,

\[
\boxed{\displaystyle 
\Delta T_f(r)=\frac{\gamma_{wi}\,V_{m,1}\,T_f^{\rm bulk}}{\Delta H_{f,1}\,r}
}
\]

or equivalently  

\[
\boxed{\displaystyle 
T_f(r)=T_f^{\rm bulk}\Bigl(1-\frac{\gamma_{wi}\,V_{m,1}}{\Delta H_{f,1}\,r}\Bigr)
}.
\]

**Assumptions used**

- The ice–water interfacial tension \(\gamma_{wi}\) is isotropic and independent of curvature.  
- The solid–liquid interface is cylindrical: one principal radius is the pore radius \(r\), the other is infinite, giving curvature \(1/r\).  
- The liquid water is incompressible; its molar volume \(V_{m,1}\) is constant.  
- The enthalpy of fusion \(\Delta H_{f,1}\) is taken as temperature‑independent near the bulk melting point.  
- The pressure difference across the curved interface follows the Laplace equation \(\Delta P=\gamma_{wi}/r\).  
- Linear expansions of the chemical potentials in temperature and pressure are adequate for the small temperature shift \(\Delta T_f\).  
- Effects of adsorption, surface chemistry, and mixture composition are ignored for this pure‑water derivation.

\]

At the temperature of maximum rate, \(T=T_p\), the derivative of the rate with respect to temperature is zero:

\[
\frac{d}{dT}\Big[\frac{d\alpha}{dT}\Big]_{T=T_p}=0 .

\Big(\frac{d\alpha}{dT}\Big)_{T_p}= \frac{A}{\beta}\exp\!\Big(-\frac{E_a}{RT_p}\Big)(1-\alpha_p),
\]

\[
\frac{E_a}{R\,T_p^{2}} = \frac{A}{\beta}\exp\!\Big(-\frac{E_a}{R T_p}\Big).
\]

\[
\beta = \frac{A R}{E_a}\,T_p^{2}\,
\exp\!\Big(-\frac{E_a}{R T_p}\Big).
\]

Taking natural logarithms yields the linear Kissinger equation:

\[
\boxed{\;\ln\!\left(\frac{\beta}{T_p^{2}}\right)=\ln\!\left(\frac{A R}{E_a}\right)-\frac{E_a}{R\,T_p}\;}

\[
\frac{d\theta}{dt}=R_{\rm ads}-k_{\rm dec}(\tau)\,\theta .

At steady state \((d\theta/dt=0)\) the adsorption flux equals the decomposition flux, giving  

\[
\boxed{\;\theta(t)=\frac{R_{\rm ads}}{k_{\rm dec}(\tau)}\; } .
\]

Because the decomposition step is the only source of surface S, the term \(k_{\rm dec}(\tau)\,\theta(t)\) in the S‑balance reduces simply to the adsorption flux:

\[
k_{\rm dec}(\tau)\,\theta(t)=R_{\rm ads}.
\]

**Surface‑S balance**

The surface concentration of S atoms obeys  

\[
\frac{dC_{s}}{dt}=k_{\rm dec}(\tau)\,\theta(t)-\frac{J_{\rm diff}}{\delta}
            =R_{\rm ads}-\frac{J_{\rm diff}}{\delta}.
\]

The diffusive flux at the surface is  

\[
J_{\rm diff}=-D(\tau)\,\Bigl.\frac{\partial C}{\partial x}\Bigr|_{x=0}.
\]

For a semi‑infinite solid with an interfacial layer of thickness \(\delta\) we may approximate the concentration gradient by a linear drop over \(\delta\),

\[
\Bigl.\frac{\partial C}{\partial x}\Bigr|_{x=0}\simeq-\frac{C_{s}(t)}{\delta},
\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad
J_{\rm diff}\simeq D(\tau)\,\frac{C_{s}(t)}{\delta}.
\]

Hence  

\[
\frac{J_{\rm diff}}{\delta}\simeq\frac{D(\tau)}{\delta^{2}}\,C_{s}(t).
\]

Substituting into the S‑balance gives the coupled ordinary differential equation for the surface S concentration:

\[
\boxed{\;\frac{dC_{s}}{dt}=R_{\rm ads}-\frac{D(\tau)}{\delta^{2}}\,C_{s}(t)\; } .
\]

\[
J_{\rm diff}(t)=\sqrt{\frac{D(\tau)}{\pi}}\,
               \int_{0}^{t}\frac{\dot C_{s}(\tau')}{\sqrt{t-\tau'}}\,d\tau' ,
\]

so that the governing equation becomes  

\[
\boxed{\;
\frac{dC_{s}}{dt}=R_{\rm ads}
-\frac{1}{\delta}\sqrt{\frac{D(\tau)}{\pi}}
   \int_{0}^{t}\frac{\dot C_{s}(\tau')}{\sqrt{t-\tau'}}\,d\tau'\; } .
\]

Either the approximate linear‑gradient form or the exact convolution form provides the required coupled differential equation in terms of the known parameters \(R_{\rm ads},\,k_{\rm dec}(\tau),\,D(\tau)\) and \(\delta\).

\Delta\nu_S\,\theta_S , & \tau\le t<2\tau,
\end{cases}

A lock‑in amplifier multiplies the signal by a sinusoidal reference at the modulation

\qquad
\int_{\tau}^{2\tau}\sin\!\Bigl(\frac{\pi t}{\tau}\Bigr)dt=-\frac{2\tau}{\pi},

\[

A_{LI}= \frac{2}{\pi}\left[

-

\[
V_i = V_{\text{BaO}}\,n_{\text{Ba}} .
\]

After conversion of half the Ba atoms to nitrate the particle contains  

\[
\frac12 n_{\text{Ba}} \text{ mol BaO} \quad\text{and}\quad
\frac12 n_{\text{Ba}} \text{ mol Ba(NO}_3)_2 .
\]

Hence  

\[
V_f = \frac12 V_{\text{BaO}}\,n_{\text{Ba}}+\frac12 V_{\text{Ba(NO}_3)_2}\,n_{\text{Ba}}
      = n_{\text{Ba}}\frac{V_{\text{BaO}}+V_{\text{Ba(NO}_3)_2}}{2}.
\]

The volume‑ratio is therefore  

\[
\frac{V_f}{V_i}= \frac{V_{\text{BaO}}+V_{\text{Ba(NO}_3)_2}}{2V_{\text{BaO}}}
               =\frac{1+V_{\text{Ba(NO}_3)_2}/V_{\text{BaO}}}{2}.
\]

With the given molar volumes  

\[
V_{\text{BaO}}=23.0\;\text{cm}^3\!\!/\text{mol},\qquad
V_{\text{Ba(NO}_3)_2}=39.5\;\text{cm}^3\!\!/\text{mol},
\]

\[
\frac{V_{\text{Ba(NO}_3)_2}}{V_{\text{BaO}}}= \frac{39.5}{23.0}=1.717,
\]

\[
\frac{V_f}{V_i}= \frac{1+1.717}{2}=1.358\;\;(\approx 1.36).
\]

Thus the model predicts a **≈ 36 % increase** in particle volume.

---

### 2.  Corresponding change in radius

Because \(V\propto R^{3}\),

\[
\frac{V_f}{V_i}= \left(\frac{R_f}{R_0}\right)^{3}
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\frac{R_f}{R_0}= \left(1.358\right)^{1/3}=1.11 .
\]

\[
\boxed{R_f \approx 1.11\,R_0\;\;(\text{about a 10 % increase in radius})}
\]

### 3.  Comparison with experiment

The STM experiment reports an **≈ 100 % (doubling) increase** in apparent particle volume after NO + O₂ dosing.  
The simple 50 % conversion model predicts only a **≈ 36 % increase** (radius increase ≈ 10 %).  

\[

* a larger fraction of BaO actually converting to nitrate,
* additional incorporation of oxygen or other species,
* morphological changes (e.g., particles becoming more spherical or porous) that increase the apparent volume,
* or experimental over‑estimation of the height in STM.

\end{aligned}

\[
f_{s}=\frac{[{\rm strong}]}{N_{\rm tot}},\qquad 
[{\rm weak}]=N_{\rm tot}(1-f_{s}).

\[
\begin{aligned}
r_{c}&=C_{1\text{-butene}}\,N_{\rm tot}\big[f_{s}k_{c,s}+(1-f_{s})k_{c,w}\big],\\[2mm]
r_{h}&=C_{1\text{-butene}}\,N_{\rm tot}\big[f_{s}k_{h,s}+(1-f_{s})k_{h,w}\big].
\end{aligned}
\]

The instantaneous propylene selectivity is

\[
S_{C3}=\frac{r_{c}}{r_{c}+r_{h}}
      =\frac{f_{s}k_{c,s}+(1-f_{s})k_{c,w}}
            {f_{s}(k_{c,s}+k_{h,s})+(1-f_{s})(k_{c,w}+k_{h,w})}.
\tag{1}
\]

\[
\begin{aligned}
k_{c,s}&=A_{c}\exp\!\Big(-\frac{E_{c,s}}{RT}\Big), &
k_{c,w}&=A_{c}\exp\!\Big(-\frac{E_{c,w}}{RT}\Big),\\[2mm]
k_{h,s}&=A_{h}\exp\!\Big(-\frac{E_{h,s}}{RT}\Big), &
k_{h,w}&=A_{h}\exp\!\Big(-\frac{E_{h,w}}{RT}\Big),
\end{aligned}
\]

\(A_{c}=1.0\times10^{6}\;{\rm s^{-1}},\;A_{h}=5.0\times10^{5}\;{\rm s^{-1}}\),
