\[
\begin{aligned}
k_{c,s}&=1.0\times10^{6}\exp\!\Big(-\frac{120\,000}{8.314\times773.15}\Big)=7.84\times10^{-3}\;{\rm s^{-1}},\\
k_{c,w}&=1.0\times10^{6}\exp\!\Big(-\frac{150\,000}{8.314\times773.15}\Big)=7.31\times10^{-5}\;{\rm s^{-1}},\\
k_{h,s}&=5.0\times10^{5}\exp\!\Big(-\frac{130\,000}{8.314\times773.15}\Big)=8.15\times10^{-4}\;{\rm s^{-1}},\\
k_{h,w}&=5.0\times10^{5}\exp\!\Big(-\frac{160\,000}{8.314\times773.15}\Big)=7.75\times10^{-6}\;{\rm s^{-1}}.
\end{aligned}
\]

Inserting these numbers into Eq. (1) gives a compact numerical form:

\[
\boxed{%
S_{C3}(f_{s})=
\frac{7.3\times10^{-5}+7.727\times10^{-3}\,f_{s}}
     {8.08\times10^{-5}+8.539\times10^{-3}\,f_{s}}
}
\tag{2}
\]

or, equivalently, in the original Arrhenius notation,

\[
\boxed{%
S_{C3}(f_{s})=
\frac{f_{s}A_{c}e^{-E_{c,s}/RT}+(1-f_{s})A_{c}e^{-E_{c,w}/RT}}
     {f_{s}\big[A_{c}e^{-E_{c,s}/RT}+A_{h}e^{-E_{h,s}/RT}\big]
      +(1-f_{s})\big[A_{c}e^{-E_{c,w}/RT}+A_{h}e^{-E_{h,w}/RT}\big]}
}.
\]

Equation (2) shows explicitly how the instantaneous propylene selectivity varies with the fraction of strong sites, \(f_{s}\). \end{aligned}
\]

Step 2 is much faster than steps 1 and 3, so the propyl radical is at quasi‑steady state:

\[
\frac{d[\mathrm{C_3H_7\cdot}]}{dt}=0\;\Rightarrow\;k_1\theta_O[\mathrm{C_3H_8}]=k_2[\mathrm{C_3H_7\cdot}]
\;\Rightarrow\;
[\mathrm{C_3H_7\cdot}]=\frac{k_1\theta_O[\mathrm{C_3H_8}]}{k_2}.
\]

Thus the rate of formation of propylene is

\[
\frac{d[\mathrm{C_3H_6}]}{dt}=0\;\Rightarrow\;k_2[\mathrm{C_3H_7\cdot}]

\[
\boxed{r_{\text{acetone}} = k_{1}\,\theta_{O}\,[\mathrm{C_{3}H_{8}}] }.
\]

\[
\frac{{\rm d}N_i}{{\rm d}t}=s_i\,F_i\Bigl(1-\frac{N_i}{N_{\,\text{site},i}}\Bigr) ,
\]

where  

* \(F_i\) – molecular flux to the surface (molecules cm\(^{-2}\) s\(^{-1}\)),  
* \(s_i\) – sticking probability (probability that a collision with a vacant site leads to adsorption),  
* \(N_{\,\text{site},i}\) – total density of adsorption sites for probe \(i\) (molecules cm\(^{-2}\)),  
* \(N_i(t)\) – number of adsorbed molecules per unit area at time \(t\).

Integrating with the initial condition \(N_i(0)=0\) gives  

\[
N_i(t)=N_{\,\text{site},i}\Bigl[1-\exp\!\Bigl(-\frac{s_i\,F_i\,t}{N_{\,\text{site},i}}\Bigr)\Bigr].
\]

The uptake coefficient is defined as  

\[
\gamma_i=\frac{N_i(\tau)}{F_i\,\tau\,A},
\qquad\text{(with }N_i\text{ per unit area, so }A\text{ cancels)},
\]

so that  

\[
\boxed{\;
\gamma_i
=\frac{N_{\,\text{site},i}}{F_i\,\tau}
\Bigl[1-\exp\!\Bigl(-\frac{s_i\,F_i\,\tau}{N_{\,\text{site},i}}\Bigr)\Bigr]
\;}
\tag{1}
\]

Equation (1) relates the measured uptake coefficient \(\gamma_i\) to the site density \(N_{\,\text{site},i}\) and the sticking probability \(s_i\).

For low coverage \((N_i\ll N_{\,\text{site},i})\) the exponential can be expanded, yielding the familiar linear approximation  

\[
\boxed{\;\gamma_i \simeq s_i\Bigl(1-\frac{N_i}{N_{\,\text{site},i}}\Bigr)\approx s_i\;},
\]

showing that in the limit of a sparsely populated surface the uptake coefficient equals the sticking probability.

The bulk temperature follows from a lumped‑mass energy balance.  
For a unit volume of the oil–catalyst mixture the microwave power density is  

\[
\dot q = \alpha |E|^{2}\qquad\bigl[\text{W m}^{-3}\bigr].
\]

If the mixture has density \(\rho\) and specific heat capacity \(c_{p}\) (so that the volumetric heat capacity is \(\rho c_{p}\) [J m\(^{-3}\) K\(^{-1}\)]), the rate of temperature increase is obtained from  

\[
\rho c_{p}\,\frac{dT}{dt}= \dot q =\alpha |E|^{2}.
\]

Hence  

\[
\frac{dT}{dt}= \frac{\alpha |E|^{2}}{\rho c_{p}} .
\]

Integrating from the initial temperature \(T_{0}\) (taken as 298 K) gives the time‑dependent temperature profile  

\[
\boxed{\,T(t)=T_{0}+\frac{\alpha |E|^{2}}{\rho c_{p}}\,t\, }.
\]

---

**Numerical evaluation (typical oil properties)**  

\[
\begin{aligned}
|E| &=5\;\text{kV m}^{-1}=5\times10^{3}\;\text{V m}^{-1},\\[2pt]
\alpha &=1.5\times10^{4}\;\text{W m}^{-3}(\text{V m}^{-1})^{-2},\\[2pt]
\dot q &=\alpha |E|^{2}=1.5\times10^{4}\,(5\times10^{3})^{2}
        =3.75\times10^{11}\;\text{W m}^{-3}.
\end{aligned}
\]

Assuming a typical heavy‑oil density \(\rho\approx 850\;\text{kg m}^{-3}\) and specific heat \(c_{p}\approx 2.0\times10^{3}\;\text{J kg}^{-1}\text{K}^{-1}\),

\[
\rho c_{p}\approx 1.7\times10^{6}\;\text{J m}^{-3}\text{K}^{-1},
\qquad
\frac{\alpha |E|^{2}}{\rho c_{p}}
\approx\frac{3.75\times10^{11}}{1.7\times10^{6}}
\approx 2.2\times10^{5}\;\text{K s}^{-1}.
\]

Thus, for this representative case  

\[
\boxed{\,T(t)\approx 298\;\text{K}+2.2\times10^{5}\,t\ \text{K},\qquad t\ \text{in seconds}\,}.
\]

The expression \(T(t)=T_{0}+(\alpha|E|^{2}/\rho c_{p})t\) is the general result; the numerical slope follows from the chosen values of \(\rho\) and \(c_{p}\).

**Modified Wulff construction**

For an orthorhombic crystal the three low‑index faces \((100),(010),(001)\) are mutually orthogonal.  
In the Wulff construction the distance \(R_{hkl}\) from the crystal centre to a face whose outward normal is \(\mathbf n_{hkl}\) satisfies  

\[
\mathbf n_{hkl}\!\cdot\!\mathbf r = \frac{\gamma_{hkl}}{\lambda},
\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad 
R_{hkl}= \frac{\gamma_{hkl}}{\lambda},
\]

where \(\lambda\) is a Lagrange multiplier fixed by the volume constraint.

---

### 1.  Polymer‑dependent surface energy of the \((010)\) face  

The fractional coverage of polymer on the \((010)\) face follows a Langmuir isotherm  

\[
\theta(c_{p})=\frac{K\,c_{p}}{1+K\,c_{p}} .
\]

The surface energy is reduced linearly with coverage:

\[
\boxed{\;
\gamma_{010}(c_{p})=
\gamma_{010}^{0}\Bigl[1-\alpha\,\theta(c_{p})\Bigr]
=
\gamma_{010}^{0}
\Bigl[1-\alpha\,\frac{K\,c_{p}}{1+K\,c_{p}}\Bigr]\; } .
\]

The other two faces are unaffected:

\[
\gamma_{100}=\gamma_{100}^{0},\qquad 
\gamma_{001}=\gamma_{001}^{0}.
\]

---

### 2.  Wulff distances

Let the half‑lengths of the equilibrium shape along the crystallographic axes be  

\[
R_{100},\;R_{010}(c_{p}),\;R_{001}.
\]

From the Wulff condition  

\[
R_{100}= \frac{\gamma_{100}^{0}}{\lambda},\qquad 
R_{010}(c_{p})= \frac{\gamma_{010}(c_{p})}{\lambda},\qquad 
R_{001}= \frac{\gamma_{001}^{0}}{\lambda}.
\tag{1}
\]

The crystal volume (a rectangular parallelepiped) is  

\[
V = (2R_{100})(2R_{010})(2R_{001}) = 8\,R_{100}R_{010}R_{001}.
\]

Using (1) one obtains  

\[
V = 8\,\frac{\gamma_{100}^{0}\,\gamma_{010}(c_{p})\,\gamma_{001}^{0}}{\lambda^{3}}
\;\;\Longrightarrow\;\;
\lambda = \Bigl[\frac{8\,\gamma_{100}^{0}\,\gamma_{010}(c_{p})\,\gamma_{001}^{0}}{V}\Bigr]^{1/3}.
\tag{2}
\]

Substituting (2) into (1) gives the explicit distances:

\[
\boxed{
\begin{aligned}
R_{100}&=\Bigl(\frac{V}{8}\Bigr)^{1/3}
\frac{\gamma_{100}^{0}}
{\bigl[\gamma_{100}^{0}\,\gamma_{010}(c_{p})\,\gamma_{001}^{0}\bigr]^{1/3}},\\[4pt]
R_{010}(c_{p})&=\Bigl(\frac{V}{8}\Bigr)^{1/3}
\frac{\gamma_{010}(c_{p})}
{\bigl[\gamma_{100}^{0}\,\gamma_{010}(c_{p})\,\gamma_{001}^{0}\bigr]^{1/3}},\\[4pt]
R_{001}&=\Bigl(\frac{V}{8}\Bigr)^{1/3}
\frac{\gamma_{001}^{0}}
{\bigl[\gamma_{100}^{0}\,\gamma_{010}(c_{p})\,\gamma_{001}^{0}\bigr]^{1/3}} .
\end{aligned}}
\]

---

### 3.  Aspect‑ratio form (often used)

Because the factor \((V/8)^{1/3}[\gamma_{100}^{0}\gamma_{010}(c_{p})\gamma_{001}^{0}]^{-1/3}\) is common to all three distances, the **relative** distances are simply proportional to the corresponding surface energies:

\[
\boxed{\;
\frac{R_{010}(c_{p})}{R_{100}}=
\frac{\gamma_{010}(c_{p})}{\gamma_{100}^{0}}
=
\frac{\displaystyle \gamma_{010}^{0}\Bigl[1-\alpha\frac{Kc_{p}}{1+Kc_{p}}\Bigr]}
{\gamma_{100}^{0}},\qquad
\frac{R_{001}}{R_{100}}=
\frac{\gamma_{001}^{0}}{\gamma_{100}^{0}} \; } .
\]

Thus the equilibrium Wulff shape remains a rectangular parallelepiped; the polymer concentration \(c_{p}\) changes only the half‑distance to the \((010)\) face through the factor \(\bigl[1-\alpha Kc_{p}/(1+Kc_{p})\bigr]\).  The other two half‑distances are independent of \(c_{p}\).

The axial site of the Co‑porphyrin can bind O₂ reversibly

\[
\mathrm{CoP}+ \mathrm{O_2}\;\rightleftharpoons\;\mathrm{CoP\!-\!O_2}
\]

with a Langmuir equilibrium constant  

\[
K=\frac{[\mathrm{CoP\!-\!O_2}]}{[\mathrm{CoP}]\;p_{\mathrm{O_2}}}\qquad(\text{units atm}^{-1}).
\]

Let \(\theta\) be the fraction of axial sites that are occupied by O₂.  
If \([C]_{\text{tot}}\) is the total concentration of CoP sites, then

\[
\begin{aligned}
[\mathrm{CoP\!-\!O_2}] &=\theta\,[C]_{\text{tot}},\\[4pt]
[\mathrm{CoP}] &= (1-\theta)\,[C]_{\text{tot}} .
\end{aligned}
\]

Insert these expressions into the definition of \(K\):

\[
K=\frac{\theta\,[C]_{\text{tot}}}{(1-\theta)\,[C]_{\text{tot}}\,p_{\mathrm{O_2}}}
   =\frac{\theta}{(1-\theta)p_{\mathrm{O_2}}}.
\]

Solve for \(\theta\):

\[
\theta = K p_{\mathrm{O_2}}(1-\theta)
\;\;\Longrightarrow\;\;
\theta\bigl(1+K p_{\mathrm{O_2}}\bigr)=K p_{\mathrm{O_2}}
\;\;\Longrightarrow\;\;
\boxed{\displaystyle \theta=\frac{K\,p_{\mathrm{O_2}}}{1+K\,p_{\mathrm{O_2}}}}.
\]

Equivalently, \(\displaystyle \theta = \frac{1}{1+1/(K p_{\mathrm{O_2}})}\). This is the Langmuir adsorption isotherm for the axial O₂ binding site.

Consider a flexible porous adsorbent that undergoes a structural “gate‑opening’’ transition only after a gas molecule adsorbs and activates the transition. The transition for gas *i* ( *i* = O₂, N₂) follows first‑order kinetics with a temperature‑dependent rate constant

\[
k_i(T)=A_i\;\exp\!\left(-\frac{E_i}{RT}\right),
\]

where *A*₁ is a pre‑exponential factor (s⁻¹) and *E*₁ is the activation energy (J mol⁻¹). Once the gate is open, the gas diffuses rapidly through the opened pores with a constant effective diffusivity *D*ᵢ (m² s⁻¹). Prior to gate opening, diffusion is negligible (the material is essentially impermeable).

A binary gas mixture at total pressure *P* and temperature *T* contacts a packed‑bed column of length *L* containing the adsorbent. The inlet gas composition is *y*₀(O₂) = *y*₀, *y*₀(N₂) = 1 − *y*₀. The gas flows as plug flow with superficial velocity *v* (m s⁻¹), giving a residence (contact) time

\[
\tau_c=\frac{L}{v}.
\]

Define the **breakthrough time** τᵢ as the time at which gas *i* first appears at the column outlet (i.e., when a measurable flux of *i* exits).

---

### (a) Derivation of breakthrough times

1. **Gate‑opening dynamics.**
   For a small element of the column, the fraction of material that has opened to gas *i* at time *t* is

   \[
   \theta_i(t)=1-\exp[-k_i t].
   \]

   Because the gate opens only after the gas adsorbs, we assume that the adsorption step is instantaneous compared with the gate‑opening step.

2. **Diffusive transport after opening.**
   Once opened, the gas diffuses a distance *L* with diffusivity *D*ᵢ. The characteristic diffusion time is

   \[
   t_{\text{diff},i}= \frac{L^{2}}{D_i}.
   \]

   Since diffusion is much faster than gate opening for O₂ (by orders of magnitude) we may neglect the diffusion time for O₂, but retain it for completeness.

3. **Breakthrough condition.**
   The outlet flux of gas *i* becomes non‑zero when the gate has opened sufficiently far downstream to allow a percolating path. A simple approximation is that breakthrough occurs when the average opened fraction reaches a critical value ≈ 1 (i.e., the gate is essentially open along the whole column). Setting

   \[
   \theta_i(\tau_i)=1-\exp[-k_i \tau_i]\approx 1,
   \]

   gives

   \[
   \tau_i \approx \frac{1}{k_i}\ln\!\left(\frac{1}{1-\theta_{\text{crit}}}\right).
   \]

   Taking \(\theta_{\text{crit}}=0.99\) (99 % opened) yields a numerical factor ≈ 4.6, so

   \[
   \boxed{\tau_i \;\approx\; \frac{4.6}{k_i(T)} \;+\; \frac{L^{2}}{D_i}}.
   \]

   The first term is the kinetic gate‑opening time, the second term the diffusive transit time after opening. For gases with very high diffusivity the second term can be omitted.

The Modified Langmuir isotherm can be written in compact form as  

\[
q(p)=\frac{q_m\,\theta}{\bigl[1+\theta^{\beta}\bigr]^{1/\beta}},\qquad 
\theta\equiv K\,\frac{p}{p_0}\; .
\]

For a data set \(\{(p_i/p_{0,i},\,q_i^{\rm exp})\}_{i=1}^{N}\) the residual vector is  

\[
r_i(\boldsymbol{\theta})=q_i^{\rm exp}-q(p_i;\boldsymbol{\theta}),\qquad 
\boldsymbol{\theta}=(q_m,\;K,\;\beta) .
\]

The Jacobian required by the Levenberg–Marquardt (LM) algorithm is the \(N\times3\) matrix  

\[
\mathbf J_{i j}= \frac{\partial q(p_i;\boldsymbol{\theta})}{\partial \theta_j},
\qquad j=1\;(q_m),\;2\;(K),\;3\;(\beta).
\]

Denoting \(\theta_i\equiv K(p_i/p_{0,i})\) and \(q_i\equiv q(p_i;\boldsymbol{\theta})\), the three partial derivatives are

\[
\boxed{
\begin{aligned}
\frac{\partial q_i}{\partial q_m}&=
\frac{\theta_i}{\bigl[1+\theta_i^{\beta}\bigr]^{1/\beta}}
\;=\; \frac{K(p_i/p_{0,i})}{\bigl[1+(K(p_i/p_{0,i}))^{\beta}\bigr]^{1/\beta}},\\[6pt]
\frac{\partial q_i}{\partial K}&=
q_m\,\frac{p_i/p_{0,i}}{\bigl[1+\theta_i^{\beta}\bigr]^{1/\beta+1}}
\;=\; \frac{q_m\,(p_i/p_{0,i})}{\bigl[1+(K(p_i/p_{0,i}))^{\beta}\bigr]^{1/\beta+1}},\\[6pt]
\frac{\partial q_i}{\partial \beta}&=
q_i\Bigg[
\frac{1}{\beta^{2}}\,
\ln\!\bigl(1+\theta_i^{\beta}\bigr)
-\frac{\theta_i^{\beta}\,\ln\theta_i}{\beta\bigl(1+\theta_i^{\beta}\bigr)}
\Bigg] \\[2pt]
&=
q_i\Bigg[
\frac{1}{\beta^{2}}\,
\ln\!\Bigl(1+\bigl[K(p_i/p_{0,i})\bigr]^{\beta}\Bigr)
-\frac{\bigl[K(p_i/p_{0,i})\bigr]^{\beta}\,
\ln\!\bigl(K(p_i/p_{0,i})\bigr)}
{\beta\Bigl(1+\bigl[K(p_i/p_{0,i})\bigr]^{\beta}\Bigr)}
\Bigg].
\end{aligned}
}
\]

Thus the Jacobian matrix for adsorbent A (or B) is obtained by evaluating the three expressions above for every experimental point \(i\) and stacking the resulting rows:

\[
\mathbf J=
\begin{bmatrix}
\displaystyle\frac{\partial q_1}{\partial q_m}&\displaystyle\frac{\partial q_1}{\partial K}&\displaystyle\frac{\partial q_1}{\partial \beta}\\[8pt]
\displaystyle\frac{\partial q_2}{\partial q_m}&\displaystyle\frac{\partial q_2}{\partial K}&\displaystyle\frac{\partial q_2}{\partial \beta}\\
\vdots&\vdots&\vdots\\
\displaystyle\frac{\partial q_N}{\partial q_m}&\displaystyle\frac{\partial q_N}{\partial K}&\displaystyle\frac{\partial q_N}{\partial \beta}
\end{bmatrix}.
\]

In the LM algorithm the parameter update \(\Delta\boldsymbol{\theta}\) is obtained from  

\[
\bigl(\mathbf J^{\!\top}\mathbf J+\lambda\,\mathrm{diag}(\mathbf J^{\!\top}\mathbf J)\bigr)\Delta\boldsymbol{\theta}
= \mathbf J^{\!\top}\mathbf r,
\]

with \(\mathbf r\) the residual vector and \(\lambda\) the damping factor.  The expressions above provide the required Jacobian entries for both adsorbents when the Modified Langmuir model is employed.

\[

\]

The number of edge atoms per unit surface area is proportional to the total perimeter \(L\) of the islands.  For compact islands of fixed shape the total perimeter scales with the square‑root of the covered area, i.e.  

\[
L=L_{0}\,\Theta^{1/2},
\]

where \(L_{0}\) is the perimeter when a full monolayer (\(\Theta=1\)) would be present.  If the spacing between edge atoms is \(a\) (≈ lattice constant), the edge‑atom density is  

\[
N_{\rm edge}= \frac{L}{a}= \frac{L_{0}}{a}\,\Theta^{1/2}=C\,\Theta^{1/2},
\]

with \(C\) a geometry factor.  The total desorption rate per unit area is then  

\[
r_{\rm des}=k(T)\,N_{\rm edge}= \nu\,C\,\Theta^{1/2}\,
\exp\!\Big(-\frac{E_{\rm des}}{RT}\Big).
\]

Absorbing the constant \(C\) into an effective pre‑exponential factor gives the coverage dependence of the desorption rate:

\[
\boxed{\,r_{\rm des}(\Theta,T)=\nu_{\rm eff}\,\Theta^{1/2}\,
\exp\!\Big(-\frac{E_{\rm des}}{RT}\Big)\,}
\]

or, equivalently,  

\[
\boxed{-\frac{d\Theta}{dt}= \nu_{\rm eff}\,\Theta^{1/2}\,
\exp\!\Big(-\frac{E_{\rm des}}{RT}\Big)} .
\]

For each step sense \(s=\pm\) the impurity coverage is  

\[
\theta_s(c)=\frac{K_s\,c}{1+K_s\,c},
\qquad 
K_s=\exp\!\Big(\frac{\varepsilon_s}{k_{\!B}T}\Big).
\]

The critical supersaturation and the kinetic coefficient become  

\[
\sigma^{*}_s=\sigma^{0}_s\bigl[1+\alpha_s\theta_s\bigr],
\qquad 
a_s=a^{0}_s\bigl[1-\beta_s\theta_s\bigr].
\]

A step moves only when \(\sigma>\sigma^{*}_s\); its normal velocity is  

\[
v_s=
\begin{cases}
a_s\bigl(\sigma-\sigma^{*}_s\bigr), & \sigma>\sigma^{*}_s,\\[4pt]
0, & \sigma\le\sigma^{*}_s .
\end{cases}
\]

Introducing the Heaviside step function \(H(x)\) (\(H(x)=1\) for \(x>0\), \(0\) otherwise), the absolute step velocity can be written as  

\[
|v_s|=H\!\bigl(\sigma-\sigma^{*}_s\bigr)\,
a^{0}_s\bigl(1-\beta_s\theta_s\bigr)
\Bigl[\sigma-\sigma^{0}_s\bigl(1+\alpha_s\theta_s\bigr)\Bigr].
\]

Since the overall normal growth rate is the sum of the absolute step velocities weighted by the step density \(\rho\),

\[
\boxed{
R(\sigma,c)=
\rho\sum_{s=\pm}
H\!\Bigl(\sigma-\sigma^{0}_s\bigl[1+\alpha_s\theta_s(c)\bigr]\Bigr)
a^{0}_s\bigl(1-\beta_s\theta_s(c)\bigr)
\Bigl[\sigma-\sigma^{0}_s\bigl(1+\alpha_s\theta_s(c)\bigr)\Bigr]
},
\]

with \(\displaystyle\theta_s(c)=\frac{K_s c}{1+K_s c}\) and \(K_s=\exp\!\bigl(\varepsilon_s/(k_{\!B}T)\bigr)\).

&\beta_+=0.4,\;\beta_-=0.3,\\
&\varepsilon_+=0.6\;\text{eV},\;\varepsilon_-=0.5\;\text{eV},\\
&T=298\;\text{K},\;k_{\!B}=8.617\times10^{-5}\;\text{eV K}^{-1},\\
&\rho=1.0\times10^{6}\;\text{m}^{-1},\qquad c=1.0\times10^{-4}\;\text{M}.
\end{aligned}
\]

\[
k_{\!B}T=8.617\times10^{-5}\times298\simeq0.02568\;\text{eV},
\]

\[
K_+=\exp\!\Bigl(\frac{0.6}{0.02568}\Bigr)\approx1.4\times10^{10},
\qquad
K_-=\exp\!\Bigl(\frac{0.5}{0.02568}\Bigr)\approx2.9\times10^{8}.
\]

Thus  

\[
\theta_+=\frac{K_+c}{1+K_+c}\approx0.9999993,\qquad

\]

Critical supersaturations  

\[

\qquad
\sigma^{*}_-=0.015\bigl[1+3\theta_-\bigr]\approx0.06.
\]

Kinetic coefficients  

\[
a_+=a^{0}_+(1-\beta_+\theta_+)\approx1.0\times10^{-6}\times0.60
=6.0\times10^{-7}\;\text{m s}^{-1},
\]
\[
a_-=a^{0}_-(1-\beta_-\theta_-)\approx0.8\times10^{-6}\times0.70

Choosing a representative supersaturation \(\sigma=0.20\) (which exceeds both \(\sigma^{*}_\pm\)), the step velocities are  

\[

\[
v_-=a_-(\sigma-\sigma^{*}_-)=5.6\times10^{-7}\,(0.20-0.06)=7.84\times10^{-8}\;\text{m s}^{-1}.

Finally  

\[
R=\rho\,(v_+ + v_-)
=1.0\times10^{6}\,(4.8\times10^{-8}+7.84\times10^{-8})
\approx1.264\times10^{-1}\;\text{m s}^{-1}.
\]

\[
\boxed{R\;\approx\;0.126\ \text{m s}^{-1}}

θ = (K_hyd c_v)/(1 + K_hyd c_v),   K_hyd = exp(β ε_h),   β = 1/(k_B T).

F_gel = (1/2) G' γ^2,

For a binary mixture that competes for the same interfacial sites the Langmuir equilibrium for each component \(i\) (\(i=p,s\)) is  

\[
K_i=\frac{\theta_i}{C_i\theta_v},
\qquad\theta_v=1-\theta_p-\theta_s,
\]

where \(\theta_i\) is the fraction of sites occupied by \(i\), \(\theta_v\) the fraction of vacant sites and \(C_i\) the bulk molar concentration.  
Hence  

\[
\theta_i=K_iC_i\theta_v .
\]

\[
\theta_p+\theta_s=(K_pC_p+K_sC_s)\theta_v .
\]

Using \(\theta_v=1-(\theta_p+\theta_s)\) and solving for \(\theta_p+\theta_s\) yields  

\[
\theta_p+\theta_s=\frac{K_pC_p+K_sC_s}{1+K_pC_p+K_sC_s}.
\]

The ratio of the two coverages follows directly from the individual equilibria:  

\[
\frac{\theta_p}{\theta_s}=\frac{K_pC_p}{K_sC_s}.
\]

Combining the ratio with the sum gives the individual fractions

\[
\theta_p=\frac{K_pC_p}{1+K_pC_p+K_sC_s},
\qquad
\theta_s=\frac{K_sC_s}{1+K_pC_p+K_sC_s}.
\]

The Langmuir constants are related to the standard free energies of adsorption by  

\[
K_i=\exp\!\Big(-\frac{\Delta G_i^{\circ}}{RT}\Big)\qquad(i=p,s),
\]

\[

   + C_s\,\exp\!\big(-\Delta G_s^{\circ}/(RT)\big)} ,\\[4pt]
\theta_s &= 
\frac{C_s\,\exp\!\big(-\Delta G_s^{\circ}/(RT)\big)}
{1+ C_p\,\exp\!\big(-\Delta G_p^{\circ}/(RT)\big)
   + C_s\,\exp\!\big(-\Delta G_s^{\circ}/(RT)\big)} .
\end{aligned}
}
\]

The two species compete for the same imprinted sites.  For a mixture of ligands the Langmuir‐type occupancy of each is  

\[
\theta_i=\frac{K\,C_i}{1+\sum_j K\,C_j}\qquad(i=A,B)
\]

so that the total fraction of occupied sites is  

\[
\theta_{\rm tot}= \theta_A+\theta_B
               =\frac{K(C_A+C_B)}{1+K(C_A+C_B)} .
\]

Because each bound molecule quenches the QD fluorescence with the same efficiency α, the measured intensity is  

\[
\boxed{\,I_{\rm mix}=I_0\Big[1-\alpha\,\theta_{\rm tot}\Big]
      =I_0\Big[1-\alpha\frac{K C_A+K C_B}{1+K C_A+K C_B}\Big]\, } .
\]

With the interferent present at a concentration ten‑times lower than the analyte,  

\[
C_B=0.1\,C_A\;\;\Longrightarrow\;\;
I_{\rm mix}=I_0\Big[1-\alpha\frac{1.1\,K C_A}{1+1.1\,K C_A}\Big].
\]

The individual intensity “contributions’’ (i.e. the quenching terms) are  

\[
I_A = I_0\,\alpha\frac{K C_A}{1+K C_A+K C_B},
\qquad
I_B = I_0\,\alpha\frac{K C_B}{1+K C_A+K C_B}
     =0.1\,I_A .
\]

Hence  

\[
\frac{I_B}{I_A}=0.1,\qquad 
\frac{C_A}{C_B}=10,
\]

and the selectivity factor defined as  

\[
S_f=\frac{C_A}{C_B}\,\frac{I_B}{I_A}
\]

becomes  

\[
\boxed{\,S_f=10\times0.1=1\,}.
\]

---

**Comment.**  
\(S_f=1\) means that the interferent B produces the same relative fluorescence change per unit concentration as the target analyte A.  Because both species have identical binding constants (K) and quenching efficiencies (α), the sensor cannot discriminate between them; the response is proportional only to the total concentration of bound species.  To achieve selectivity, the MIP must be designed so that \(K_A\neq K_B\) or \(\alpha_A\neq\alpha_B\).

For a given type of site (the β‑sites) the competitive Langmuir adsorption is  

\[
\theta_{\rm CO}= \frac{K_{\rm CO}P_{\rm CO}}
{1+K_{\rm CO}P_{\rm CO}+K_{\rm CH_3OH}P_{\rm CH_3OH}} .
\]

Because the CO dose is low, \(K_{\rm CO}P_{\rm CO}\ll 1\) and the denominator can be written as  

\[
1+K_{\rm CH_3OH}P_{\rm CH_3OH}\; .
\]

Thus  

\[
\theta_{\rm CO}\approx\frac{K_{\rm CO}P_{\rm CO}}
{1+K_{\rm CH_3OH}P_{\rm CH_3OH}} .
\]

The TPD β‑peak intensity \(I\) is proportional to the amount of CO adsorbed on the β‑sites, i.e. to \(\theta_{\rm CO}\).  
For the clean stepped surface (no methanol)  

\[
I_{0}\propto K_{\rm CO}P_{\rm CO}.
\]

With pre‑adsorbed methanol  

\[
I_{\rm meth}\propto \frac{K_{\rm CO}P_{\rm CO}}
{1+K_{\rm CH_3OH}P_{\rm CH_3OH}} .
\]

The experiment shows \(I_{\rm meth}=0.5\,I_{0}\), therefore  

\[
\frac{1}{1+K_{\rm CH_3OH}P_{\rm CH_3OH}} = 0.5
\;\;\Longrightarrow\;\;
1+K_{\rm CH_3OH}P_{\rm CH_3OH}=2
\;\;\Longrightarrow\;\;
K_{\rm CH_3OH}P_{\rm CH_3OH}=1 .
\]

The fractional coverage of the β‑sites by methanol is  

\[
\theta_{\rm CH_3OH}= \frac{K_{\rm CH_3OH}P_{\rm CH_3OH}}
{1+K_{\rm CH_3OH}P_{\rm CH_3OH}}
= \frac{1}{1+1}=0.5 .
\]

Hence 50 % of the β‑sites are blocked by methanol.  

\[
\boxed{0.5}
\]

u(z)=\frac{z}{\mu}\,\frac{\partial\gamma}{\partial r}.

Evaluating at the free surface \(z=h(r,t)\) gives the radial surface velocity  

\[
u_{s}(r,t)=u(z=h)=\frac{h(r,t)}{\mu}\,\frac{\partial\gamma}{\partial r}.
\]

(If a pressure gradient \(\partial p/\partial r\) were retained, the full expression would be

The van der Waals–Platteeuw model treats each hydrate cage as a single‑site adsorption site that can be empty or occupied by one guest molecule.  
For a given cage type \(j\) the grand‑canonical partition function is  

\[
\Xi_{j}=1+\sum_{i}C_{i,j}\,f_{i},
\]

where \(C_{i,j}\) is the Langmuir constant for guest \(i\) in cage \(j\) and \(f_{i}\) is the fugacity of species \(i\) (for an ideal gas \(f_{i}\approx p_{i}\)).  

The probability (fractional occupancy) that a cage of type \(j\) is occupied by guest \(i\) is the ratio of the term in \(\Xi_{j}\) corresponding to that guest to the whole partition function:

\[
\boxed{\displaystyle 
\theta_{i,j}= \frac{C_{i,j}\,f_{i}}{1+\sum_{k}C_{k,j}\,f_{k}}
}\;.
\]

Assuming ideal‑gas behaviour (\(f_{i}=p_{i}=y_{i}P_{\text{tot}}\)), the expressions for the two guests become  

\[
\boxed{\displaystyle 
\theta_{\text{He},j}= \frac{C_{\text{He},j}\,p_{\text{He}}}
{1+C_{\text{He},j}\,p_{\text{He}}+C_{\text{Ar},j}\,p_{\text{Ar}}},\qquad
\theta_{\text{Ar},j}= \frac{C_{\text{Ar},j}\,p_{\text{Ar}}}
{1+C_{\text{He},j}\,p_{\text{He}}+C_{\text{Ar},j}\,p_{\text{Ar}}}
}\;,
\]

with \(j=5^{12}\) (small cage) or \(j=5^{12}6^{2}\) (large cage) and  

\[
p_{\text{He}}=0.8\,P_{\text{tot}},\qquad 
p_{\text{Ar}}=0.2\,P_{\text{tot}} .
\]

answer:
The SFG intensity from a spherical droplet of radius \(R\) follows  

\[
I_{\text{SFG}}^{\text{sphere}}(R)=C(R)\,\bigl|\chi_{\text{eff}}^{(2)}\bigr|^{2},
\qquad 
C(R)=\frac{1}{1+(k_{\text{IR}}R)^{2}} .
\]

---

### 1.  Water contribution  

For a charged interface the average dipole orientation obeys the Gouy‑Chapman relation  

\[
\chi_{\text{water}}^{(2)}=\alpha\,E_{s}
      =\alpha\,\frac{\sigma}{\varepsilon_{0}\varepsilon_{r}} .
\]

The surface charge density is related to the surface (zeta) potential by  

\[
\sigma=\varepsilon_{0}\varepsilon_{r}\,\kappa\,\psi_{0}
      \;\;\;\text{with}\;\;\psi_{0}\simeq\zeta .
\]

Hence  

\[
\chi_{\text{water}}^{(2)}=\alpha\,\kappa\,\zeta(p\!H).
\]

---

### 2.  Ionic (adsorbed \(\mathrm{OD}^{-}\)) contribution  

The surface coverage of adsorbed hydroxide follows a Langmuir isotherm  

\[
\theta(p\!H)=\frac{K\,c_{\mathrm{OH}^{-}}}{1+K\,c_{\mathrm{OH}^{-}}},\qquad
c_{\mathrm{OH}^{-}}=10^{-(14-p\!H)}\;{\rm M},
\]

so that  

\[
\chi_{\text{ion}}^{(2)}=\beta\,\theta(p\!H)
      =\beta\,\frac{K\,10^{-(14-p\!H)}}{1+K\,10^{-(14-p\!H)}} .
\]

---

### 3.  Total effective susceptibility  

\[
\chi_{\text{eff}}^{(2)}(p\!H)=\chi_{\text{water}}^{(2)}+\chi_{\text{ion}}^{(2)}
   =\alpha\,\kappa\,\zeta(p\!H)
    +\beta\,\frac{K\,10^{-(14-p\!H)}}{1+K\,10^{-(14-p\!H)}} .
\]

---

### 4.  Final expression for the spherical‑droplet SFG intensity  

\[
\boxed{
I_{\text{SFG}}^{\text{sphere}}(R,p\!H)=
\frac{1}{1+(k_{\text{IR}}R)^{2}}\,
\Bigg[
\alpha\,\kappa\,\zeta(p\!H)
+\beta\,\frac{K\,10^{-(14-p\!H)}}{1+K\,10^{-(14-p\!H)}}
\Bigg]^{2}
}
\]

where  

\[
\begin{aligned}
&\alpha =5\times10^{-12}\ {\rm m/V},\qquad
\beta =2\times10^{-12}\ {\rm m/V},\\[2pt]
&\kappa =\frac{1}{0.3\ {\rm nm}}=3.33\times10^{9}\ {\rm m^{-1}},\\[2pt]
&k_{\text{IR}}=\frac{2\pi}{2.8\;\mu{\rm m}}=2.245\times10^{6}\ {\rm m^{-1}},\\[2pt]
&K =10^{2}\ {\rm M^{-1}},\qquad
\zeta(p\!H)=\zeta_{7}+(\zeta_{11}-\zeta_{7})\frac{p\!H-7}{4},
\;\;(\zeta_{7}=-10\ {\rm mV},\ \zeta_{11}=-30\ {\rm mV}) .
\end{aligned}
\]

The term in brackets contains the Gouy‑Chapman water contribution (first term) and the possible \(\mathrm{OD}^{-}\) ionic contribution (second term); the prefactor \(C(R)=\bigl[1+(k_{\text{IR}}R)^{2}\bigr]^{-1}\) accounts for curvature of the droplet.

**Derivation**

At equilibrium between the gas phase and the adsorbed phase  

\[
\mu_{\text{gas}}=\mu_{\text{ads}} .
\]

For an ideal gas  

\[
\mu_{\text{gas}}=\mu^{\circ}_{\text{g}}(T)+RT\ln\!\frac{p}{p^{\circ}} .
\]

For the adsorbed layer at fixed coverage θ the change of the chemical potential with temperature is related to the isosteric heat of adsorption \(Q_{st}\) :

\[
d\mu_{\text{ads}}=-Q_{st}\,d\!\left(\frac{1}{T}\right) .
\]

Equating the differentials of the two chemical potentials (since θ is held constant) gives  

\[
RT\,d\ln p =-Q_{st}\,d\!\left(\frac{1}{T}\right) .
\]

Hence  

\[
d\ln p =-\frac{Q_{st}}{R}\,d\!\left(\frac{1}{T}\right) .
\]

Integrating between two points \((p_1,T_1)\) and \((p_2,T_2)\) that correspond to the **same** coverage θ,

\[
\int_{p_1}^{p_2} d\ln p = -\frac{Q_{st}}{R}\int_{1/T_1}^{1/T_2} d\!\left(\frac{1}{T}\right) ,
\]

\[
\ln\!\frac{p_2}{p_1}= -\frac{Q_{st}}{R}\,\Bigl(\frac{1}{T_2}-\frac{1}{T_1}\Bigr) .
\]

Solving for the isosteric heat of adsorption yields the familiar Clausius–Clapeyron form

\[
\boxed{\,Q_{st}= -R\,
\frac{\ln(p_2/p_1)}{\,1/T_2-1/T_1\,}
= -R\left(\frac{\partial\ln p}{\partial(1/T)}\right)_{\theta}\,} .
\]

Thus, by measuring the equilibrium vapor pressure \(p\) at two temperatures \(T_1\) and \(T_2\) that give the same surface coverage \(\theta\), the isosteric heat of adsorption \(Q_{st}\) can be obtained directly from the above expression.

The gas in the bed occupies only the void volume  

\[
V_{\rm void}= \varepsilon\,V_{\rm bed}\;,
\]

so that, for an ideal gas, the total number of moles present at pressure \(P\) and temperature \(T\) is  

\[
n_{\rm gas}= \frac{P\,V_{\rm void}}{R\,T}
          =\frac{\varepsilon\,V_{\rm bed}\,P}{R\,T}\; .
\]

---

### (i)  Vacuum step (evacuation from \(P_b\) to \(P_l\) at \(T_d\))

The minimum reversible work for an isothermal evacuation is  

\[
W_{\rm vac}= \int_{P_b}^{P_l} n_{\rm gas}\,R\,T_d\,d\ln P
           = n_{\rm gas}(P_b)\,R\,T_d\ln\!\frac{P_b}{P_l}
           =\frac{\varepsilon V_{\rm bed}P_b}{R\,T_d}\,R\,T_d\ln\!\frac{P_b}{P_l}
           =\varepsilon V_{\rm bed}P_b\ln\!\frac{P_b}{P_l}.
\]

Specific energy (per kilogram of adsorbent)  

\[
E_{\rm vac}= \frac{W_{\rm vac}}{m_{\rm ads}}
           =\frac{\varepsilon V_{\rm bed}P_b}{m_{\rm ads}}\,
             \ln\!\frac{P_b}{P_l}.
\]

---

### (ii)  Heating step (raising the gas from \(T_a\) to \(T_d\) at constant \(P_b\))

The number of moles present at the start of heating (at \(T_a\)) is  

\[
n_i =\frac{\varepsilon V_{\rm bed}P_b}{R\,T_a}.
\]

Heating the gas to \(T_d\) while maintaining the pressure (the excess gas is vented at \(T_d\)) requires a sensible‑heat input  

\[
Q_{\rm heat}= n_i\,C_{p,\rm mix}\,(T_d-T_a)
            =\frac{\varepsilon V_{\rm bed}P_b\,C_{p,\rm mix}}{R\,T_a}\,
              (T_d-T_a).
\]

Specific heating energy  

\[
E_{\rm heat}= \frac{Q_{\rm heat}}{m_{\rm ads}}
            =\frac{\varepsilon V_{\rm bed}P_b\,C_{p,\rm mix}}{m_{\rm ads}\,R\,T_a}\,
              (T_d-T_a).
\]

---

\[
\boxed{
\begin{aligned}
E_{\rm vac}&=\frac{\varepsilon V_{\rm bed}P_b}{m_{\rm ads}}\,
            \ln\!\Bigl(\frac{P_b}{P_l}\Bigr) ,\\[4pt]
E_{\rm heat}&=\frac{\varepsilon V_{\rm bed}P_b\,C_{p,\rm mix}}{m_{\rm ads}\,R\,T_a}\,
              \bigl(T_d-T_a\bigr) .
\end{aligned}}
\]

(If the bulk density \(\rho_{\rm bulk}=m_{\rm ads}/V_{\rm bed}\) is known, the factor \(\varepsilon V_{\rm bed}/m_{\rm ads}\) can be written as \(\varepsilon/\rho_{\rm bulk}\).)

**Derivation**

In the BET model the adsorption of the first molecular layer is characterized by an equilibrium constant \(K_{1}\) and the adsorption of any subsequent layer (i.e. condensation on the already‑covered surface) by an equilibrium constant \(K_{L}\).

For a process \(i\) the temperature dependence of its equilibrium constant follows the van’t Hoff relation  

\[
\frac{d\ln K_{i}}{d(1/T)}=-\frac{\Delta H_{i}}{R}\;,
\]

which integrates (assuming \(\Delta H_{i}\) is temperature‑independent) to  

\[
\ln K_{i}= -\frac{\Delta H_{i}}{RT}+{\rm const}.
\]

Thus  

\[
K_{1}= \exp\!\Big(-\frac{\Delta H_{\rm ads}}{RT}\Big),\qquad
K_{L}= \exp\!\Big(-\frac{\Delta H_{\rm liq}}{RT}\Big).
\]

The BET constant \(C\) is defined as the ratio of these two equilibrium constants:

\[
C\;=\;\frac{K_{1}}{K_{L}}
   \;=\;\exp\!\Big[-\frac{\Delta H_{\rm ads}}{RT}
                   +\frac{\Delta H_{\rm liq}}{RT}\Big]
   \;=\;\exp\!\Big(\frac{\Delta H_{\rm ads}-\Delta H_{\rm liq}}{RT}\Big).
\]

Hence  

\[
\boxed{\,C=\exp\!\Big(\dfrac{\Delta H_{\rm ads}-\Delta H_{\rm liq}}{R\,T}\Big)\,}.
\]

---

\[
\Delta H_{\rm ads}=45\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1},\qquad
\Delta H_{\rm liq}=30\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1},\qquad
R=8.314\ \text{J mol}^{-1}\text{K}^{-1},\qquad
T=298\ \text{K}.
\]

\[
C=\exp\!\Big(\frac{(45-30)\times10^{3}\ {\rm J\,mol^{-1}}}
                 {8.314\times298\ {\rm J\,mol^{-1}K^{-1}}}\Big)
  =\exp(6.05)\approx4.3\times10^{2}.
\]

\[
\boxed{C\approx4.3\times10^{2}}.
\]

For a single F–Si pair the REDOR intensity follows  

\[
\frac{S}{S_{0}}=\cos(b\tau)\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad 
b=\frac{\arccos(S/S_{0})}{\tau}.
\]

| \(\tau\) (µs) | \(S/S_{0}\) | \(\arccos(S/S_{0})\) (rad) | \(b=\arccos(S/S_{0})/\tau\) (rad s\(^{-1}\)) |
|--------------|------------|----------------------------|--------------------------------------------|
| 20 | 0.84 | 0.571 | \(0.571/(20\times10^{-6}) = 2.86\times10^{4}\) |
| 40 | 0.66 | 0.850 | \(0.850/(40\times10^{-6}) = 2.13\times10^{4}\) |
| 60 | 0.48 | 1.070 | \(1.070/(60\times10^{-6}) = 1.78\times10^{4}\) |
| 80 | 0.32 | 1.244 | \(1.244/(80\times10^{-6}) = 1.55\times10^{4}\) |

Because the values vary slightly (experimental noise), a linear fit of \(\theta_i=\arccos(S_i)\) versus \(\tau_i\) (forced through the origin) gives the best‑fit slope

\[
b_{\text{fit}}=\frac{\sum\tau_i\theta_i}{\sum\tau_i^{2}}
               =\frac{20(0.571)+40(0.850)+60(1.070)+80(1.244)}
                      {20^{2}+40^{2}+60^{2}+80^{2}}
               =0.0174\;\text{rad µs}^{-1}
               =1.74\times10^{4}\;\text{rad s}^{-1}.
\]

We will use this value (the mean of the four individual estimates is \(2.08\times10^{4}\) rad s\(^{-1}\); the two are within 20 % and give the same distance to within 0.1 Å).

**Step 2 – Relate \(b\) to the internuclear distance \(r\)**  

For a heteronuclear dipolar interaction between two spin‑½ nuclei  

\[
b=\frac{\mu_{0}}{4\pi}\,
   \frac{\gamma_{F}\,\gamma_{\text{Si}}\,\hbar}{r^{3}} .
\]

Insert the constants (use absolute values for the gyromagnetic ratios):

\[
\begin{aligned}
\frac{\mu_{0}}{4\pi}&=10^{-7}\;\text{N·A}^{-2},\\
\gamma_{F}&=2.518\times10^{8}\;\text{rad s}^{-1}\,\text{T}^{-1},\\
|\gamma_{\text{Si}}|&=5.313\times10^{7}\;\text{rad s}^{-1}\,\text{T}^{-1},\\
\hbar&=1.0545718\times10^{-34}\;\text{J·s}.
\end{aligned}
\]

The numerator is  

\[
N=\frac{\mu_{0}}{4\pi}\,\gamma_{F}\,\gamma_{\text{Si}}\,\hbar
  =10^{-7}\,(2.518\times10^{8})(5.313\times10^{7})(1.0545718\times10^{-34})
  \approx 1.41\times10^{-25}\; \text{(SI units)} .
\]

Solve for \(r^{3}\):

\[
r^{3}= \frac{N}{b}
     = \frac{1.41\times10^{-25}}{1.74\times10^{4}}
     \approx 8.1\times10^{-30}\;\text{m}^{3}.
\]

Take the cube root:

\[
r = (8.1\times10^{-30})^{1/3}
  \approx 2.0\times10^{-10}\;\text{m}
  = 2.0\;\text{Å}.
\]

\[
\boxed{r \approx 2.0\ \text{Å}}

\end{aligned}

\frac{k_{\text{M}^1}}{k_{\text{M}^2}}

\[

\[
\frac{k_{\text{M}^1}}{k_{\text{M}^2}}
   = \exp\!\Bigl[-\frac{4.0\times10^{4}}{(8.314)(298)}\Bigr]
   = \exp(-16.2) \approx 9.6\times10^{-8}.
\]

Thus  

\[
k_{\text{M}^1} \approx 1\times10^{-7}\,k_{\text{M}^2},
\qquad
k_{\text{M}^2} \approx 10^{7}\,k_{\text{M}^1}.
\]

\[
\boxed{\displaystyle \frac{k_{\text{M}^1}}{k_{\text{M}^2}}\;\approx\;1\times10^{-7}\;\text{(i.e., M}^{2}\text{ degrades about }10^{7}\text{ times faster than M}^{1}\text{ at 298 K)}}.

\[
\mathrm{*NO+*O \;\xrightarrow{k_{\rm RDS}}\; *NO_2+*}
\]

so that the instantaneous rate of NO₂ formation per surface site is  

\[
r = k_{\rm RDS}\,\theta_{\rm NO}\,\theta_{\rm O}\qquad (1)
\]

### 1.  Adsorption equilibria  

\[
\begin{aligned}
\theta_{\rm NO}&=K_{\rm NO}\,p_{\rm NO}\,\theta_* ,\\[2pt]
\theta_{\rm O}&=\bigl(K_{\rm O_2}\,p_{\rm O_2}^{1/2}\bigr)^{1/2}\,\theta_* ,\\[2pt]
\theta_{\rm NO_2}&=K_{\rm NO_2}\,p_{\rm NO_2}\,\theta_* .
\end{aligned}
\tag{2}
\]

Define  

\[
\alpha_O\equiv\bigl(K_{\rm O_2}\,p_{\rm O_2}^{1/2}\bigr)^{1/2}
          =\sqrt{K_{\rm O_2}}\;p_{\rm O_2}^{1/4}.
\tag{3}
\]

---

### 2.  Site balance  

\[
\theta_*+\theta_{\rm NO}+\theta_{\rm O}+\theta_{\rm NO_2}=1 .
\]

Using (2),

\[
\theta_*\bigl[1+K_{\rm NO}p_{\rm NO}+\alpha_O+K_{\rm NO_2}p_{\rm NO_2}\bigr]=1,
\]

hence  

\[
\theta_*=\frac{1}{D},\qquad 
D\equiv 1+K_{\rm NO}p_{\rm NO}+\alpha_O+K_{\rm NO_2}p_{\rm NO_2}.
\tag{4}
\]

Consequently  

\[
\theta_{\rm NO}= \frac{K_{\rm NO}p_{\rm NO}}{D},\qquad
\theta_{\rm O}= \frac{\alpha_O}{D}.
\tag{5}
\]

---

### 3.  Rate expression  

Insert (5) into (1):

\[
r = k_{\rm RDS}\,\frac{K_{\rm NO}p_{\rm NO}\,\alpha_O}{D^{2}}.
\tag{6}
\]

The rate constant of the RDS follows the Arrhenius law  

\[
k_{\rm RDS}=A\exp\!\Big(-\frac{E_a}{RT}\Big),
\tag{7}
\]

with the activation energy given by the BEP relation  

\[
E_a = \alpha\,\Delta E_{\rm rxn}+\beta,
\qquad 
\Delta E_{\rm rxn}=E_{*{\rm NO}}+E_{*{\rm O}}-E_{*{\rm NO_2}} .
\tag{8}
\]

Because the adsorption energy of *NO₂ is the same on all facets \((E_{*{\rm NO_2}}=-1.80\;{\rm eV})\) and the adsorption energy of *NO is facet‑independent, the facet dependence of the barrier resides only in the atomic‑oxygen adsorption energy \(E_{*{\rm O}}\).  Using \(\alpha=0.5,\;\beta=0.8\;{\rm eV}\),

\[
E_a = 0.5\bigl(E_{*{\rm NO}}+E_{*{\rm O}}+1.80\bigr)+0.8
     = 0.5\,E_{*{\rm O}}+C,
\tag{9}
\]

where \(C=0.5\,E_{*{\rm NO}}+1.7\;{\rm eV}\) is a constant common to all facets.

---

### 4.  Final steady‑state rate law  

Combining (6)–(9) gives the desired expression for the rate of NO₂ formation on a given Pt facet:

\[
\boxed{
r \;=\; A\,
\exp\!\Big[-\frac{E_a}{RT}\Big]\;
\frac{K_{\rm NO}\,p_{\rm NO}\,
\bigl(K_{\rm O_2}\,p_{\rm O_2}^{1/2}\bigr)^{1/2}}
{\Big[\,1+K_{\rm NO}p_{\rm NO}
      +\bigl(K_{\rm O_2}\,p_{\rm O_2}^{1/2}\bigr)^{1/2}
      +K_{\rm NO_2}p_{\rm NO_2}\Big]^{2}}
}
\]

with  

\[
E_a = 0.5\bigl(E_{*{\rm NO}}+E_{*{\rm O}}+1.80\bigr)+0.8\;{\rm eV}
      \;=\;0.5\,E_{*{\rm O}}+C .
\]

Thus the rate depends on the gas‑phase partial pressures, the adsorption equilibrium constants, and the facet‑dependent activation energy through the oxygen adsorption energy \(E_{*{\rm O}}\).

**(a) Derivation**

For the dual‑site Langmuir model the excess uptake on each site is  

\[
q_i(p,T)=q_i^{\max }\;\frac{b_i(T)\,p}{1+b_i(T)\,p}\qquad(i=A,B) .
\]

Define  

\[
B_i\equiv b_i(T)p ,\qquad 
\theta_i\equiv\frac{B_i}{1+B_i}\;(=q_i/q_i^{\max }) .
\]

---

**Step 1 – Derivatives of the single‑site term**

\[
\frac{\partial q_i}{\partial p}=q_i^{\max }\frac{b_i(T)}{[1+b_i(T)p]^2}
      =\frac{q_i^{\max }b_i(T)}{(1+B_i)^2},
\tag{1}
\]

\[
\frac{\partial q_i}{\partial T}=q_i^{\max }\,
      \frac{p\,\partial b_i/\partial T}{(1+B_i)^2}.
\tag{2}
\]

The temperature dependence of the Langmuir constant is taken as the
van ’t Hoff form  

\[
b_i(T)=b_{i,0}\,\exp\!\Big(\frac{E_i}{RT}\Big) ,
\]

where the (negative) parameter \(E_i\) is the adsorption energy.
Hence  

\[
\frac{\partial b_i}{\partial T}=b_i(T)\,\frac{E_i}{R\,T^{2}} .
\tag{3}
\]

Inserting (3) into (2) gives  

\[
\frac{\partial q_i}{\partial T}
   =\frac{E_i}{R\,T^{2}}\;p\;
     \frac{q_i^{\max }b_i(T)}{(1+B_i)^2}
   =\frac{E_i}{R\,T^{2}}\;p\;
     \frac{\partial q_i}{\partial p}.
\tag{4}
\]

---

**Step 2 – Clausius–Clapeyron relation at constant total loading**

The total excess uptake is  

\[
q(q,p,T)=q_A(p,T)+q_B(p,T) .
\]

At a fixed value of \(q\) the pressure and temperature are linked by  

\[
f(p,T)=q_A(p,T)+q_B(p,T)-q=0 .
\]

Differentiating implicitly (constant \(q\)):

\[
\frac{\partial f}{\partial p}\,\frac{dp}{dT}
   +\frac{\partial f}{\partial T}=0
\;\Longrightarrow\;
\frac{dp}{dT}=-
\frac{\partial q_A/\partial T+\partial q_B/\partial T}
     {\partial q_A/\partial p+\partial q_B/\partial p}.
\tag{5}
\]

The isosteric heat follows from the Clausius–Clapeyron equation  

\[
Q_{st}= -R\Bigl(\frac{\partial\ln p}{\partial(1/T)}\Bigr)_{q}
      = R\,T^{2}\frac{dp/dT}{p}.
\tag{6}
\]

Substituting (5) into (6) and using (4) yields  

\[
Q_{st}= -\,\frac{E_A\,\partial q_A/\partial p
               +E_B\,\partial q_B/\partial p}
              {\partial q_A/\partial p+\partial q_B/\partial p}.
\tag{7}
\]

---

**Step 3 – Explicit form in terms of the model parameters**

From (1)  

\[
\frac{\partial q_i}{\partial p}
   =\frac{q_i^{\max }\,b_i(T)}{[1+b_i(T)p]^2},
\qquad i=A,B .
\]

Inserting these expressions into (7) gives the isosteric heat as a
function of pressure (and temperature) :

\[
\boxed{
Q_{st}(p,T)=
-\frac{
      E_A\,q_A^{\max }\,b_A(T)\,[1+b_A(T)p]^{-2}
     +E_B\,q_B^{\max }\,b_B(T)\,[1+b_B(T)p]^{-2}}
     {q_A^{\max }\,b_A(T)\,[1+b_A(T)p]^{-2}
     +q_B^{\max }\,b_B(T)\,[1+b_B(T)p]^{-2}} } .
\tag{8}
\]

---

**Step 4 – Expression as a function of the total uptake \(q\)**  

Using the site loadings  

\[
q_i = q_i^{\max }\frac{b_i p}{1+b_i p}
     \;\;\Longrightarrow\;\;
b_i p = \frac{q_i}{q_i^{\max }-q_i},
\]

the derivative (1) can be rewritten as  

\[
\frac{\partial q_i}{\partial p}
   =\frac{q_i\big(q_i^{\max }-q_i\big)}{p\,q_i^{\max }} .
\]

Therefore (7) becomes a weighted average of the site energies with
weights proportional to \(q_i(q_i^{\max }-q_i)/q_i^{\max }\):

\[
\boxed{
Q_{st}(q)=
-\frac{
   E_A\,\dfrac{q_A\big(q_A^{\max }-q_A\big)}{q_A^{\max }}
 + E_B\,\dfrac{q_B\big(q_B^{\max }-q_B\big)}{q_B^{\max }}}
 {\dfrac{q_A\big(q_A^{\max }-q_A\big)}{q_A^{\max }}
 +\dfrac{q_B\big(q_B^{\max }-q_B\big)}{q_B^{\max }}} } ,
\qquad q_A+q_B=q .
\tag{9}
\]

Equation (8) (or equivalently (9)) is the required explicit expression
for the isosteric heat of adsorption as a function of the total excess
uptake for the dual‑site Langmuir model. The heat is a weighted average
of the site‑specific adsorption energies, the weights being set by the
differential capacities of the two sites at the given loading.

& R_R^{0}=r_{H_2}+R_{CH}^{0}=2.1+1.05=3.15\;{\rm mol\,H_2\,s^{-1}}\\[4pt]
\text{Cat‑K: } & r_{H_2}=2.8,\; \text{CH}_4\text{ rate}=0.10\;\Rightarrow\; 
R_{CH}^{K}=3\times0.10=0.30,\\
& R_R^{K}=2.8+0.30=3.10\;{\rm mol\,H_2\,s^{-1}} .
\end{aligned}
\]

Hence  

\[
\frac{k_{RF}^{K}}{k_{RF}^{0}}=\frac{R_R^{K}}{R_R^{0}}=
\frac{3.10}{3.15}=0.984 .
\]

With the Arrhenius form \(k=A\exp(-E_a/RT)\) and equal pre‑exponential factors,

\[
\frac{k_{RF}^{K}}{k_{RF}^{0}}=

\[

\;\;\Longrightarrow\;\;
\Delta E_{a,R}=E_{a,R}^{K}-E_{a,R}^{0}= -RT\ln(0.984)
=8.085\;{\rm kJ\,mol^{-1}}\times0.0162\approx0.13\;{\rm kJ\,mol^{-1}} .
\]

Thus the reforming activation energy is essentially unchanged; Cat‑K is only ~0.1 kJ mol⁻¹ higher.

The adsorption constant for CO follows  

\[
K_{CO}=K_0\exp\!\Big(-\frac{\Delta H_{\rm ads}}{RT}\Big) ,

with \(\Delta H_{\rm ads}\) taken as the strong‑site desorption energy from CO‑TPD:

\[
\Delta H_{\rm ads}^{0}=150\;{\rm kJ\,mol^{-1}},\qquad
\Delta H_{\rm ads}^{K}=130\;{\rm kJ\,mol^{-1}} .
\]

Hence  

\[
\frac{K_{CO}^{K}}{K_{CO}^{0}}=
\exp\!\Big[\frac{\Delta H_{\rm ads}^{0}-\Delta H_{\rm ads}^{K}}{RT}\Big]
=\exp\!\Big[\frac{20\,000}{8.314\times973}\Big]
=\exp(2.47)\approx 11.8 .
\]

From the rates above  

\[
\frac{R_{CH}^{K}}{R_{CH}^{0}}=
\frac{0.30}{1.05}=0.2857 .
\]

Therefore  

\[
\frac{k_{CH}^{K}}{k_{CH}^{0}}=
\frac{R_{CH}^{K}}{R_{CH}^{0}}\,
\frac{K_{CO}^{0}}{K_{CO}^{K}}
=0.2857\;\times\;\frac{1}{11.8}=0.0238 .
\]

Using the Arrhenius relation for the methanation constant,

\[
\frac{k_{CH}^{K}}{k_{CH}^{0}}=
\exp\!\Big[-\frac{E_{a,CH}^{K}-E_{a,CH}^{0}}{RT}\Big] .

Metal sites:  \(\theta_*+\theta_{C_{16}H_{34}*}+\theta_{H*}\simeq1\).

\theta_* \simeq 1-\theta_{C_{16}H_{34}*}.

\[
\theta_{C_{16}H_{34}*}=K_{1}p_{C_{16}}\,(1-\theta_{C_{16}H_{34}*})

\boxed{\;\theta_{C_{16}H_{34}*}= \frac{K_{1}\,p_{C_{16}}}{1+K_{1}\,p_{C_{16}}}\;}\tag{3}

Support vacancies:  \(\theta_{\square}+\theta_{OH\,\square}\simeq1\).

r_{H_2}=r_{2}=k_{2}\,[C_{16}H_{34}*]
        =k_{2}\,\theta_{C_{16}H_{34}*}\,C_{M}.
\]

Because the dehydrogenation of the adsorbed alkane requires a neighboring
hydroxyl on the oxide support, the probability that a C₁₆H₃₄* species is
adjacent to an OH□ is proportional to the hydroxyl coverage \(\theta_{OH\,\square}\).
Hence the effective rate is proportional to the product of the two coverages

\[
r_{H_2}=k_{2}\,C_{M}\,C_{V}\,\theta_{C_{16}H_{34}*}\,\theta_{OH\,\square}.
\]

4. **Insert the Langmuir coverages (3) and (2)**

\[
\boxed{

        \frac{K_{1}\,p_{C_{16}}}{1+K_{1}\,p_{C_{16}}}\;
        \frac{K_{3}\,p_{H_{2}O}}{1+K_{3}\,p_{H_{2}O}}
      } \tag{4}
\]

5. **Simplified form (low to moderate coverages)**  

If the surface is not heavily covered (\(K_{1}p_{C_{16}}\ll1,\;K_{3}p_{H_{2}O}\ll1\)),
the product of the two denominators can be linearised, giving the compact
Langmuir–Hinshelwood expression

\[
\boxed{
r_{H_2}\;\approx\;
\frac{k_{2}\,C_{M}\,C_{V}\,K_{1}\,K_{3}\,p_{C_{16}}\,p_{H_{2}O}}
     {1+K_{1}\,p_{C_{16}}+K_{3}\,p_{H_{2}O}}
      } \tag{5}
\]

---

* Intermediates C₁₆H₃₃*, C₁₆H₃₂O* and surface H* are assumed to have negligible
  steady‑state coverages because steps 4–6 are fast.
* The hydrogen coverage on metal (\(\theta_{H*}\)) is taken as very small,

* Metal‑site balance is reduced to \(\theta_*+\theta_{C_{16}H_{34}*}\approx1\);

* For the compact form (5) the product term \(K_{1}K_{3}p_{C_{16}}p_{H_{2}O}\) in the
  denominator is neglected (low‑coverage limit).

The resulting expression (4) (or its low‑coverage approximation (5)) gives the
overall H₂‑formation rate as a function of the reactant partial pressures,
the equilibrium constants, the intrinsic rate constant of the RDS, and the
concentrations of metal and vacancy sites.
